## Codex · 2026-06-10T03:27:09.758Z · final_answer

Because the thing you rerouted is probably not the thing AT’s voice router is actually using.

There are only a few realistic explanations:

1. **You changed the Events URL, not the Voice Callback URL.**
   AT’s own docs distinguish them: Callback URL controls the call flow (`<Play>`, `<Record>`); Events URL just receives status updates. If Events is correct but Callback is stale, the call still dies.

2. **There is an app-level Voice callback overriding the phone-number callback.**
   The phone number page can show `eduforequality.org`, but the Voice app/config may still have `short-waves-rule.loca.lt`. The call-hop “To:” field is the truth.

3. **You changed the right UI field, but AT’s routing backend/cache did not update.**
   This is plausible because your dashboard reportedly showed the correct URL while the actual call hop still went to the tunnel.

4. **Wrong app/environment.**
   AT has sandbox vs production app contexts. If `+2342017001459` lives under one app but you changed callback settings in another app, the UI can look “fixed” while the live number routes elsewhere.

What I verified just now:
`https://eduforequality.org/api/sabi/at/incoming` works.
`https://eduforequality.org/api/sabi/at/incoming?fresh=1` works.
`https://eduforequality.org/api/sabi/at/events?fresh=1` works.
`https://short-waves-rule.loca.lt/...` is dead with 503.

So the next move is not code. In AT, check the **latest failed call’s Voice Session Hops**:

- If `To:` still says `short-waves-rule.loca.lt`, AT did not actually reroute the live voice callback.
- If `To:` says `eduforequality.org` and still fails, send me that exact hop response/status because that would be a different bug.

## Codex · 2026-06-10T03:35:37.150Z · final_answer

I checked the current AT docs. My read: **we are not obviously on the wrong Nigeria voice plan**, but we may be using the wrong AT primitive for live AI conversation.

What the docs say:

- AT Voice is available in **Nigeria**. Source: [Countries offering Voice Product](https://help.africastalking.com/en/articles/11532624-countries-offering-voice-product)
- The **Voice sandbox is not operational**; they tell people to request a live test number. So using a real/test number is expected. Source: [Voice Sandbox](https://help.africastalking.com/en/articles/11532610-voice-sandbox)
- A **callback URL** is for call actions like `Play`/`Say`; an **events URL** is for call events. Source: [Callback URL vs Events URL](https://help.africastalking.com/en/articles/5947806-what-is-the-difference-between-a-callback-url-and-an-events-url)
- Their official SDK documents `<Record callbackUrl="...">` as “URL to forward the results of the Recording action.” Source: [Africa’s Talking PHP SDK](https://github.com/AfricasTalkingLtd/africastalking-php/blob/master/README.md)
- But their help article describes `<Record>` as recording a call session into a file “that you can then retrieve and play later,” which sounds more asynchronous than real-time voice-agent style. Source: [What audio formats are supported by record](https://help.africastalking.com/en/articles/2948319-what-audio-formats-are-supported-by-record)

So the answer is: **AT docs imply recording callbacks exist, but they do not clearly prove AT supports a live record -> webhook -> return new XML -> play -> record loop on your Nigeria test number.** Your real call log shows it did **not**: it delivered `recordingUrl` only after `callSessionState: Completed`.

I already deployed one last compatibility patch: the XML now includes both `callbackUrl` and `callBackUrl`. If the next call still posts the recording only after `Completed`, then this is not a plan issue we can fix in code. It means AT’s `<Record>` path for this number/product is post-call recording, not live conversational recording.

The exact question for AT support is:

```text
Does Africa's Talking Nigeria Voice support an in-call <Record> loop where:
1. our callback returns <Play> + <Record callbackUrl="...">
2. AT records caller speech
3. AT POSTs recordingUrl to callbackUrl while the call is still active
4. our callback returns another <Say>/<Play> + <Record>
5. the same call continues?

Our current Nigeria test number only sends recordingUrl after callSessionState=Completed, so the call is already over.
Is live Record -> callback -> XML continuation supported on this number type, or do we need SIP/VAPI/a different voice product?
```

My honest recommendation: test once more with the patch. If hop 2 still goes to `/incoming` after `Completed`, stop fighting AT for live AI tutoring and use Twilio/ElevenLabs/SIP for the conversational path.

8. “Can AT SIP-trunk this Nigerian number to our own PBX/Asterisk server? Docs mention callback URL format `trunk:IP`. Is that available for our number, and what are the Nigeria SIP incoming/outgoing rates?”

**Twilio Cost Stack**
Current Twilio pricing is higher than our old research.

Twilio Nigeria outbound:
- To Nigeria local: **$0.2303/min**
- To Nigeria mobile: **$0.2349/min**
Source: [Twilio Nigeria Voice pricing](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/voice/pricing/ng)

Twilio US inbound:
- Local number inbound: **$0.0085/min**
- US local number: **$1.15/month**
Source: [Twilio US Voice pricing](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/voice/pricing/us)

Twilio AI-ish extras:
- Conversation Relay: **$0.07/min**
- Media Streams: **$0.004/min**
- Gather speech recognition: **$0.018/use** default, **$0.025/use** Deepgram/Google v2
Source: [Twilio Nigeria Voice pricing](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/voice/pricing/ng)

So if Twilio calls Nigerian mobiles directly, a 6-minute call is about:

`6 * $0.2349 = $1.41` voice only.

With Conversation Relay:

`6 * ($0.2349 + $0.07) = $1.83/call`, before LLM/TTS extras.

For 150 kids, 20 calls/month, 6 min/call:

`150 * 20 * 6 * $0.2349 = ~$4,228/month` voice only.

That’s why Twilio direct-to-Nigeria is not the cheap pilot path.

**Can AT Forward Nigerian Calls To Twilio?**
Probably yes technically, if AT supports `<Dial>` to the Twilio US number. But it is likely a bridge with double charging:

- child pays to call Nigerian AT number unless it is toll-free
- AT charges/handles the Nigerian inbound leg
- AT charges you to dial/bridge onward to the US Twilio number
- Twilio charges inbound US minutes
- Twilio then charges whatever AI stack you use

So: possible for a demo, probably bad for scale.

The better ask is not “can you forward to Twilio number?” It’s: **“Can you SIP trunk the Nigerian number to our PBX or a SIP endpoint so we get live bidirectional audio?”** AT’s own SIP help says they can connect to a PBX and use callback format `trunk:trunk_ip_address`. Source: [AT SIP trunk setup](https://help.africastalking.com/en/articles/6049012-what-do-i-need-to-set-up-a-sip-trunk-connection)

My recommendation: use the AT engineer call to force a yes/no on live `<Record>` looping. If no, ask for SIP trunking immediately.

## Naomi · 2026-06-10T03:45:47.912Z

what's KYC?

## Codex · 2026-06-10T03:45:52.548Z · final_answer

KYC means **Know Your Customer**.

It is the verification process a telecom/payment/platform provider uses before giving you regulated services like phone numbers, SIP trunks, bulk messaging, payments, or toll-free lines.

For Africa’s Talking / Nigerian voice service, KYC probably means they may ask for things like:

- your organization/legal name
- founder or authorized representative ID
- business/nonprofit registration documents, if available
- address/contact details
- intended use case for the number
- signed request letter or service agreement

Basically: “prove who you are and what you’re using this phone infrastructure for,” so they can comply with telecom rules and prevent fraud/spam.

## Codex · 2026-06-10T05:06:37.048Z · final_answer

Honestly: maybe **20-40% chance he responds**, and if he does, likely within **2-7 days**.

Why it could work: the email is personal, specific, founder-to-founder, and you’re not asking for “advice” vaguely. You’re bringing a real mission, traction, and a concrete collaboration/co-founder possibility.

Why he might not: he may be busy, employed/contracted somewhere, wary of “co-founder” language from someone he doesn’t know yet, or just bad at email. Builders like him often live more on LinkedIn/X/WhatsApp than Gmail.

Best move: if no reply in **3-4 days**, send a short LinkedIn/X message that says you emailed him and would love to speak. If no reply after **7 days**, send one gentle email follow-up.

## Codex · 2026-06-11T18:58:38.791Z · commentary

I’m going to separate two things here: what number format will route, and who pays what. I’ll first check our telephony research/pricing notes, then I’ll verify anything rate-related against current sources because call pricing is exactly the kind of thing that drifts.

## Codex · 2026-06-11T18:59:07.539Z · final_answer

If they’re **inside Nigeria**, they should be able to dial the local/national version:

`0201 700 1459`

That is the Nigerian trunk-prefix format for our `+234 201 700 1459` number. The `+234` becomes `0` when dialing from inside Nigeria. If they’re outside Nigeria, they must use `+2342017001459`.

Cost-wise:

- **To Sabi/our AT account:** if the call is answered, Africa’s Talking SIP incoming is **₦3/min**. So:
  - 1 min = ₦3
  - 5 min = ₦15
  - 7 min = ₦21
  - 37 seconds = about ₦1.85, exactly what we saw before.

- **To the child/family:** unless it’s a toll-free `0800` line or we use flash-callback, they pay their normal carrier voice tariff for calling a Lagos/geographic number. That varies by carrier/plan. It is **not free** just because they dial `0201...`.

- **If you meant `0800`:** that is the toll-free-style path in Nigeria, but our current AT number is **not** an `0800` number. It’s a regular Lagos-style `0201` number.

The code is okay for both `+2342017001459` and digit-only versions now. The bigger user-cost question is product design: for children, we still want flash-callback so they “beep” us, hang up/unanswered, and then Sabi calls them back.

## Codex · 2026-06-12T17:00:37.878Z · final_answer

Telephony-only, using Africa’s Talking Nigeria SIP pricing:

**$80 ≈ ₦110k-₦113k today.** Wise shows about ₦1,376/$, black-market sources show about ₦1,409/$.

AT Nigeria voice pricing says **SIP incoming/outgoing is ₦3/min** and regular outgoing is **₦15/min**.

So on AT SIP:

| Lesson length | Kids served with $80 |
|---|---:|
| 5 min each | ~7,300 kids |
| 10 min each | ~3,600 kids |
| 15 min each | ~2,400 kids |
| 20 min each | ~1,800 kids |

If we subtract the AT monthly number fee, listed as **₦5,000 + 7.5% VAT = ₦5,375**, then it is more like:

| Lesson length | Kids served after number fee |
|---|---:|
| 5 min each | ~6,900 kids |
| 10 min each | ~3,490 kids |
| 15 min each | ~2,330 kids |
| 20 min each | ~1,745 kids |

For comparison, on **Twilio calling Nigerian phones** at about **$0.2349/min**, $80 only buys ~340 minutes, so:

- 10-minute lessons: **~34 kids**
- 15-minute lessons: **~22 kids**

So the AIVA line is: **“At Nigeria-local SIP rates, $80 can support roughly 3,500 ten-minute voice lessons, compared with only about 34 ten-minute calls through standard international Twilio-to-Nigeria routing.”**

## Codex · 2026-06-14T19:07:24.695Z · final_answer

To make true spoken interruption possible, we need to stop treating the phone call like:

`play full audio -> record answer -> process -> play full audio`

and turn it into:

`listen continuously while Sabi speaks -> detect caller speech -> stop Sabi instantly -> capture new utterance -> respond`

Right now AGI can’t do that because `STREAM FILE` plays audio and `RECORD FILE` records audio as separate blocking steps.

The best path is:

1. Move Asterisk call control from **AGI** to **ARI/Stasis**.
   ARI is Asterisk’s app-control API for channels/bridges/media, instead of one dialplan command at a time. Official docs describe ARI as exposing channels, bridges, endpoints, and media primitives: [Asterisk ARI overview](https://docs.asterisk.org/Configuration/Interfaces/Asterisk-REST-Interface-ARI/).

2. Use **ExternalMedia** or **AudioSocket** to stream call audio into our Python service.
   Asterisk has `/channels/externalMedia` for sending call media to an external app: [External Media and ARI](https://docs.asterisk.org/Development/Reference-Information/Asterisk-Framework-and-API-Examples/External-Media-and-ARI/). AudioSocket is also built for real-time audio frames over TCP: [AudioSocket docs](https://docs.asterisk.org/Configuration/Channel-Drivers/AudioSocket/).

3. Run realtime VAD on the caller audio.
   While Sabi is speaking, the service keeps listening. If it detects Naomi/child speech above threshold for maybe 200-400ms, it cancels Sabi playback.

4. Make Sabi’s TTS cancellable.
   Instead of generating one full WAV and playing it, we stream or chunk TTS. When caller speech starts, we stop playback, flush queued audio, and move into listening mode.

5. Then optimize the AI stack for realtime turns.
   Local Whisper batch transcription is okay for today, but true “website demo feel” wants streaming STT or short VAD-cut utterances. ElevenLabs streaming TTS or chunked TTS also helps.

My recommended build order:

- **Now:** keep current AGI path, no beep, faster silence-stop, `#` interrupt.
- **Next prototype:** ARI + AudioSocket/ExternalMedia for one call, just prove live audio frames reach Python while Sabi audio plays.
- **Then:** add VAD-based barge-in cancellation.
- **Then:** replace full-file TTS playback with chunked/streaming TTS.

So: yes, totally possible. But it’s a phone media architecture change, not a setting inside the current AGI loop.

## Codex · 2026-06-14T19:10:19.140Z · final_answer

For a working prototype: **1 long focused day**.

For something I’d trust for demos/submissions: **2-3 days**.

Breakdown:

- **2-4 hours:** add ARI config, route calls into `Stasis`, prove Python can control the call.
- **4-8 hours:** stream live call audio via AudioSocket/ExternalMedia into Python.
- **4-6 hours:** add VAD so caller speech interrupts Sabi playback.
- **4-8 hours:** make TTS playback cancellable/chunked enough to feel natural.
- **half day:** test against Africa’s Talking weirdness, logging, failure recovery, cleanup.

The riskiest part is not the AI. It’s Asterisk media plumbing and making sure AT’s SIP/RTP behaves cleanly once we move from the simpler AGI flow to realtime media.

If we need “works tonight,” I’d keep the current path and polish latency. If we need “feels like the website demo on phone,” budget **2-3 days**.

## Naomi · 2026-06-15T16:14:23.180Z

## Codex · 2026-06-15T16:14:46.140Z · final_answer

Because those `[laugh]`, `[chuckle]`, `[sigh]` things were just text instructions, not actual audio controls in the path we’re using.

In this call, logs show we used **ElevenLabs TTS first**. That endpoint takes text and speaks it. It doesn’t interpret `[laugh]` as “insert a real laugh”; it often just reads the word aloud, especially in a phone/narrowband conversion path.

So:

`Yes! [laugh] You got it!`

became something like:

“yes laugh you got it”

instead of:

“yes! hahaha, you got it!”

Chatterbox has been described as supporting expressive/nonverbal tags, but our deployed Chatterbox Turbo path has already shown signs that some expressivity controls are ignored or unreliable. And right now it is fallback after ElevenLabs, so ElevenLabs gets the text first.

To make her actually laugh/chuckle/sigh, we’d need one of these:

1. **Use a TTS model that truly supports nonverbal tags** and put it first in the phone path.
2. **Pre-generate laugh/chuckle/sigh audio clips** in Sabi’s voice, then splice them into responses.
3. **Use natural prosody instead of literal nonverbals**, which is what I changed it to for now: “Yeees, you got it!” instead of `[laugh]`.

For premium UX, I think option 2 is the most controllable: small tasteful laugh/sigh clips, inserted only when needed, never read aloud.

## Codex · 2026-06-15T16:49:57.648Z · final_answer

The easiest credible path is **not** “write a whole new curriculum.” It is:

**Make Sabi a standards-mapped FLN intervention.**

Meaning: Sabi teaches foundational literacy/numeracy, and every skill/lesson is mapped to NERDC, Cambridge, TaRL, and GPF. That is much easier, cleaner, and more defensible than trying to become a full school curriculum immediately.

**Best Formalization Stack**
1. **NERDC = Nigerian anchor**
   Use official NERDC Basic Education Curriculum pages/PDFs as the national reference, especially Primary 1-3 and Primary 4-6 Mathematics/English.

2. **Global Proficiency Framework = measurement anchor**
   Use UNESCO/UIS GPF for minimum proficiency in reading/math. This makes Sabi legible to funders, World Bank/UNICEF-style people, and learning-outcomes reviewers.

3. **TaRL = placement + remediation method**
   Keep diagnostic placement by ability, not age/grade. This is perfect for out-of-school or enrolled-but-not-learning children.

4. **Cambridge = international quality benchmark**
   Use Cambridge Primary as a high-bar comparison, especially for scope/sequence and progression, but do not claim Cambridge certification.

5. **Sabi = delivery layer**
   Voice-first lessons, app/print bridge where needed, adaptive mastery tracking.

**The Practical Workflow**
1. Build a spreadsheet/database curriculum map:
   `Sabi skill -> lesson -> assessment item -> NERDC ref -> Cambridge ref -> GPF level -> TaRL level -> delivery mode`.

2. Start with **Foundational Numeracy**:
   It is the cleanest because voice can genuinely teach counting, operations, money, mental arithmetic, and word problems.

3. Then do **Oral Literacy Phase 1**:
   Phonemic awareness, vocabulary, listening comprehension, oral grammar. Be honest that print reading requires app/print support.

4. Add an educator review packet:
   10-15 pages: philosophy, scope/sequence, standards crosswalk, sample lessons, assessments, limitations.

5. Get a Nigerian curriculum expert/teacher/LASUBEB-adjacent reviewer to sign off:
   Not “NERDC approved,” but “reviewed for alignment with NERDC Basic Education Curriculum.” That’s probably the easiest credible formal validation.

**What I Can’t Do Alone**
- I can’t certify it as NERDC-approved.
- I can’t certify Cambridge alignment officially.
- I can’t replace an expert Nigerian curriculum reviewer if you need institutional credibility.
- I can’t honestly make voice-only literacy equal to full reading/writing instruction without print/app materials.

**Sources I Checked**

- Cambridge Primary consultant: to review whether our Cambridge crosswalk is accurate.
- Assessment reviewer: EGRA/EGMA/ASER/NALABE-style measurement.

Right now AT’s job is basically: route `+2342017001459` to our SIP trunk at `136.243.8.51`, and allow outbound from that IP. The real-time conversation/barge-in is on our Asterisk + AudioSocket code.

The questions I’d ask AT now:

1. **Outbound format**
   “For outbound SIP calls from `136.243.8.51`, what exact SIP URI / caller ID format should we use? Is `PJSIP/+234XXXXXXXXXX@africastalking` with From user `+2342017001459` correct?”

2. **Call duration cap**
   “Are there any default maximum call duration limits or test-account limits on this DID/SIP trunk? We saw one call end around 3 minutes during testing.”

3. **RTP/media IPs**
   “Will RTP always come from `102.223.37.68`, or do you use separate media IP ranges we should whitelist?”

4. **Concurrent calls / rate limits**
   “What are the current concurrent call limits and calls-per-second limits for this trunk/DID?”

5. **Billing**
   “Please confirm inbound and outbound Nigeria voice rates, billing increment, VAT, failed-call charging, and whether SIP inbound/outbound has the same price as normal Voice API.”

6. **DID permanence**
   “Is `+2342017001459` now a permanent/prod DID on our account, or still a test number with expiry?”

7. **Zero-cost child experience**
   “Do you offer Nigerian toll-free/0800, reverse-billed, sponsored, or zero-rated calling options for education/nonprofit use? If yes, what is the provisioning path and pricing?”

8. **Production monitoring**
   “Can you provide SIP failure reasons/CDRs beyond the dashboard, or a webhook/API for call status and SIP disconnect causes?”

The most important ones are **duration cap, outbound SIP format, RTP IP ranges, and pricing**.

## Codex · 2026-06-15T17:05:18.968Z · final_answer

Yes. **It is possible for Cambridge to review us directly, but only through specific routes.** The best route is **Cambridge International “Endorsed resources”**, not “Cambridge accreditation.”

**The Real Cambridge Routes**

1. **Cambridge International Endorsed Resource**
This is the most relevant. Cambridge says publishers/providers can submit resources for review, including **EdTech companies, not-for-profits, universities, and print/digital publishers**. If accepted, Cambridge subject experts review the resource against criteria like alignment to the Cambridge framework, assessment quality, international suitability, and whether it promotes effective teaching/learning.

Outcome: we could potentially say something like **“Cambridge International endorsed resource for Cambridge Primary Mathematics/English”** if granted.

Contact: `publisher.relations@cambridge.org`

Source: [Cambridge endorsement guide PDF](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/748803-a-guide-to-the-cambridge-international-education-endorsement-process.pdf), [Endorsed resources page](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/support-and-training-for-schools/endorsed-resources/)

2. **Cambridge Partnership for Education**
This is bigger and more consultancy-like. They work with ministries and international development organisations on curriculum design, assessment design, teacher training, system review, and sometimes alignment/certification. They reviewed Ethiopia’s curriculum reform and Bhutan received a Cambridge **Certificate of Alignment** through a national education reform partnership.

Outcome: possible curriculum/assessment review or attestation, but likely expensive and more institutional than the resource-endorsement route.

Source: [Cambridge Partnership for Education](https://www.cambridge.org/partnership), [Ethiopia case study](https://www.cambridge.org/partnership/case-studies/ethiopia), [Bhutan alignment case](https://www.cambridge.org/gb/partnership/news-and-events/news/bhutan-and-cambridge-mark-major-milestone-in-national-education-reform)

**My Recommendation**

Start with **Cambridge International Publisher Relations**, not Cambridge Partnership. Ask:

> We are a not-for-profit EdTech developing a voice-first foundational literacy and numeracy resource for Nigerian learners, mapped to Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 and English 0058/0057. Are we eligible to submit a digital/voice learning resource for Cambridge International endorsement? If yes, what endorsement category, fees, timeline, and submission materials apply?

Then separately ask Cambridge Partnership whether they offer a smaller curriculum/assessment alignment review for nonprofit EdTech pilots.

Important: we still should not say **“Cambridge accredited curriculum.”** The realistic win is **“submitted for Cambridge International resource endorsement”** or, if successful, **“Cambridge International endorsed resource.”**

## Codex · 2026-06-15T17:08:23.035Z · final_answer

Yes. Deep-research answer: **Cambridge can review us directly, but the route matters a lot.**

The earlier “Cambridge can’t accredit a self-authored curriculum” is still true if we mean **Cambridge-accredited curriculum**. But current Cambridge materials show a more useful path: **Cambridge International can review and potentially endorse teaching/learning resources from EdTech companies and not-for-profits.** That means E4E/Sabi may be eligible to submit a packaged resource for review.

**Best Route**
**Cambridge International Endorsed Resources**

This is the strongest fit. Cambridge’s April 2026 endorsement guide says eligible submitters include:

- publishers
- EdTech companies
- not-for-profit organisations
- universities

They accept ad hoc applications, and the first step is emailing Publisher Relations / submitting the endorsement application. They review against:

- support for a Cambridge syllabus or curriculum framework
- target audience/market need
- alignment with curriculum
- appropriate assessment coverage
- teacher support
- innovation
- Cambridge textbook/resource development principles
- EDIB/inclusion

Source: [Cambridge endorsement guide PDF](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/748803-a-guide-to-the-cambridge-international-education-endorsement-process.pdf), [Endorsed resources page](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/support-and-training-for-schools/endorsed-resources/)

**Important nuance:** this is not “Cambridge approves our whole curriculum as an official Cambridge curriculum.” It would be more like: **“Sabi / Education for Equality resource endorsed by Cambridge International to support Cambridge Primary Mathematics/English.”**

**Likelihood for Us**
For the **web curriculum app / Grade 4 Cambridge-aligned materials**: realistic if we package it properly.

For **Sabi voice-only foundational literacy/numeracy**: possible, but trickier. We need to position it as a **digital learning resource / learner support / teacher support / alternative delivery medium** mapped to Cambridge Primary Math 0096 and English/ESL 0058/0057. Pure “AI tool” may be harder; a structured resource with fixed lessons, teacher guide, assessment, and accessibility documentation is much stronger.

**Other Cambridge Routes**
1. **Cambridge Partnership for Education**
They do curriculum review/design/development, especially with ministries, NGOs, and development organisations. They explicitly say they can review/evaluate drafts and help improve curriculum frameworks. This is likely a paid consultancy route, not a quick badge.

Source: [Cambridge Partnership curriculum services](https://www.cambridge.org/partnership/our-services/curriculum)

2. **Cambridge assessment accreditation / attestation**
If we build formal assessments or qualifications, Cambridge Partnership says they can accredit/attest assessment programmes and qualifications after review. This is heavier and probably later.

Source: [Cambridge assessment services](https://www.cambridge.org/partnership/our-services/assessment)

3. **Cambridge Mathematics**
They offer mathematics curriculum review/development for a unique context. This could be excellent for our numeracy pathway, but likely consultancy, not public endorsement.

Source: [Cambridge Mathematics curriculum development](https://www.cambridgemaths.org/our-services/curriculum-development/)

**What I’d Do**
Email Cambridge International **now** and ask eligibility. Don’t overbuild before they tell us what category fits.

Draft:

```text
Subject: Eligibility question: Cambridge Primary endorsement for nonprofit EdTech resource

Dear Cambridge Publisher Relations team,

My name is Naomi Ivie, founder of Education for Equality, a nonprofit EdTech initiative building foundational literacy and numeracy tools for Nigerian learners.

We are developing Sabi, a voice-first AI learning resource for children who may not have reliable internet or smartphones, alongside a web curriculum app. Our materials are being mapped to Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 and Cambridge Primary English / English as a Second Language 0058/0057, with Nigerian contextualisation and foundational-learning scaffolding.

I saw in the April 2026 Cambridge International endorsement guide that EdTech companies and not-for-profit organisations may submit resources for review. Could you please confirm whether a digital/voice learning resource like ours may be eligible for Cambridge International endorsement?

If yes, could you advise:
1. which endorsement category would fit best,
2. whether Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 and English/ESL 0058/0057 are eligible frameworks for this submission,
3. what materials we should prepare,
4. the review fees and expected timeline,
5. whether dynamic/AI-supported resources can be reviewed if the curriculum, lesson scripts, assessment items, and teacher guidance are fixed and documented?

Kind regards,
Naomi Ivie
Founder, Education for Equality
```

Bottom line: **yes, ask Cambridge directly.** The door is more open than the old research suggested, especially because the 2026 guide explicitly includes EdTech and nonprofits. But we should ask for **endorsement/review**, not “accreditation.”

## Codex · 2026-06-15T19:51:31.019Z · final_answer

In principle, yes: if the call reaches the AT DID `+2342017001459`, Sabi will now immediately reject/hang up the inbound leg and call back the caller ID it receives.

But two caveats:

- The caller ID must arrive in a callback-able format, like `+1860...` or `+234...`. If the carrier hides or mangles caller ID, Sabi cannot call back correctly.
- AT outbound must be allowed/rated for that destination country. It is enabled for your IP, but international callback routes may behave differently by country/carrier.

So: any number in the world can *try* to trigger callback, but reliability will depend on caller ID delivery and AT’s outbound route to that country. For real Nigerian kids calling from Nigerian SIMs, it should be much cleaner than your current US/test-phone setup.

For each app, call `+2342017001459`, then check AT sessions:

- If AT shows caller as your real `+1` number and Sabi calls back, the app works.
- If AT shows anonymous/relay/weird caller ID, discard that app.
- If Nigerian callers work but one US app sounds weird, that app is the problem, not Sabi.

## Codex · 2026-06-15T21:50:39.335Z · final_answer

Yes, but for **our exact Sabi test**, a Nigerian number has to do two things:

1. Call `+2342017001459` and show a real callback number.
2. Receive Sabi’s callback.

That rules out a lot of “virtual number” products.

**Best Practical Options**

**1. Real Nigerian SIM via tester: best**
This is the cleanest. MTN/Airtel/Glo/9mobile SIM behaves like an actual child’s phone. Since someone in Nigeria already called and it worked, this is the gold-standard test path.

Set up 3 testers:
- one MTN
- one Airtel
- one Glo or 9mobile

Pay them small airtime/test stipend. This is faster and more accurate than buying weird VoIP products.

**2. Your own Nigerian SIM/eSIM: possible, but not easy remotely**
A real Nigerian SIM generally needs SIM registration/NIN. MTN says SIM registration requires presenting a VNIN/NIN slip, and MTN eSIM activation is done through the normal SIM registration/swap process. Airtel Nigeria says eSIM activation requires a service centre / physical SIM path. So from the US, this is not likely to be instant self-service.

**3. Nigerian virtual number: maybe, but risky**
Providers like CloudTalk, AVOXI, Global Call Forwarding, Telnyx, DIDLogic advertise Nigerian virtual numbers. But many are business DIDs for receiving/forwarding calls, not true mobile SIMs. The danger is the same Rebtel problem: the callback may go to a gateway, forwarding number, or SIP trunk rather than a real handset.

Before buying, ask them:

> Can this Nigerian number make an outbound PSTN call to `+2342017001459` with the purchased `+234` number as caller ID, and can it receive a normal inbound PSTN callback from `+2342017001459`?

If they say “inbound forwarding only,” skip it.

**4. Travel eSIMs: probably not enough**
Some Nigeria eSIM pages advertise “data, calls, SMS,” but many eSIMs are data-only or app-calling only. For Sabi, app-calling is not enough. It needs a real callable phone number.

**My recommendation**
For today: use Nigerian testers. For ongoing development: keep a small Nigeria tester panel instead of trying to simulate Nigeria from the US. For your own “personal test number,” only buy a virtual number after the provider confirms real outbound caller ID + inbound callback.

Sources: [MTN SIM registration](https://www.mtn.ng/sim/sim-registration-tips/), [MTN eSIM](https://www.mtn.ng/helppersonal/esim/), [Airtel eSIM](https://www.airtel.com.ng/ng/personal/services/sim-services/esim), [AVOXI Nigeria numbers](https://www.avoxi.com/nigeria-virtual-phone-numbers/), [Global Call Forwarding Nigeria numbers](https://www.globalcallforwarding.com/services/virtual-phone-numbers/nigeria-virtual-phone-numbers/), [CloudTalk Nigeria virtual number](https://www.cloudtalk.io/virtual-number-nigeria/)

- **Nigerian local/virtual number**: easiest to buy online; can give `+234` caller ID and softphone access, but it is not a real MTN/Airtel/Glo SIM.
- **Nigerian 0800 toll-free number**: best production UX because kids call free and stay connected, but usually business/provider provisioning.

Most promising for testing now. They say they offer local and toll-free Nigeria numbers, local caller ID, inbound/outbound, IVR, call forwarding, and no setup/contracts. Use case: buy a Nigerian local number, call Sabi from AVOXI softphone with `+234` caller ID, then answer Sabi’s callback inside AVOXI.

2. **Telnyx**
Cheapest developer-style option. Nigeria local numbers start at `$1/month`, and you assign the number to SIP. Good for engineering, but may require account verification and setup. Not toll-free.

3. **DIDWW**
Strong technical option. Nigeria local numbers support inbound calls and SIP trunking for outbound; Lagos `+234 201` exists. But “registration required,” so likely not instant.

Nigerian CPaaS options. Sendchamp has virtual numbers for calling/receiving and IVR. HollaTags says it supports outbound calls, dedicated local numbers, and IVR. These are likely more legit Nigerian routes, but probably sales/onboarding.

5. **Yana / IntarvAS / Alpha / Outsource Nigeria**
These are the more “real Nigerian 0800/0700/Special Number” providers. Best for production toll-free:
- Yana is NCC-licensed for Special Numbering Services and offers 0800, 0700, short codes.
- IntarvAS offers 0700/0800 smart numbers and PBX.
- Alpha offers SMAT numbers, 0800/0700, and a caller app.
- Outsource Nigeria offers 0800 lines covering all networks.

Not “right now,” but these are the people to contact for the actual toll-free production number.

For production: pursue **0800 toll-free** through **Yana, IntarVas, Alpha, or AVOXI**.

## Codex · 2026-06-15T22:59:51.943Z · final_answer

Yes, you were right. I checked the call before the last one, and Sabi messed up.

In that call, Sabi asked:

`500 naira, 100 naira per bag. How many bags can you buy?`

Your answer came through STT as:

`Five hundred, five bucks.` then `Five bugs.` then `Five bugs.`

That should have been accepted as **five bags**. The answer matcher can extract the number `5`, but the realtime phone loop was letting the LLM judge the raw weird transcript too literally. So Sabi treated “bugs/bucks” like confusion instead of recognizing the intended numeric answer.

I fixed and deployed it live:

- [voice_realtime.py](/Users/naomiivie/Education%20for%20Equality/sabi-server/voice_realtime.py): numeric answers now pass through even when STT confidence is low, so “twenty naira” won’t get rejected just because Whisper is nervous.
- [voice_realtime.py](/Users/naomiivie/Education%20for%20Equality/sabi-server/voice_realtime.py): if Sabi asked about bags, “bugs/bucks” gets normalized to “bags.”
- [llm.py](/Users/naomiivie/Education%20for%20Equality/sabi-server/llm.py): Sabi is now explicitly instructed to grade the intended number first and tolerate phone transcript weirdness.

Verified live in Docker:

`Five bugs.` → numeric answer detected, normalized to `Five bags.`
`Twenty naira.` → numeric answer detected
`Betsy Naira` → not falsely treated as a number

Hi Samuel,

The inbound rejection you saw was intentional in our earlier flash-callback test path. Direct Nigeria-originating calls have worked successfully on our side. The only confusing behavior we were investigating was with international calling apps like Yolla/Rebtel, where the caller heard brief prerecorded “hello” audio even though our PBX rejected the test leg.

Please feel free to test inbound again now. If you still see a rejection from our side, kindly share the timestamp/session details and we will trace it immediately.

Yours sincerely,
Naomi Ivie

## Codex · 2026-06-16T21:32:23.965Z · final_answer

You’re right: Termii is bigger than “OTP voice.” My read after checking their current site/docs is:

**Confirmed Termii Can Do**
- SMS via API, including transactional/DND and promotional routes.
- SMS Sender ID registration/status.
- WhatsApp messaging, including media support.
- Email/product notifications.
- Automated voice delivery: text-to-speech voice calls for alerts/verification-style messages.
- Voice pricing exists: `$0.0102/min`, plus `$10` monthly voice subscription, `$1.70` Direct Inward Dialing number, `$2` voice channel.
- AI/workflow routing across SMS, WhatsApp, email, and voice.
- “Resolve” product claims inbound voice calls can be triaged/responded to autonomously.
- Sotel/eSIM API for data connectivity, not relevant to phone-call Sabi except as adjacent telecom infra.

**Not Publicly Confirmed Yet**
- SIP trunking to our Asterisk PBX.
- Inbound Nigerian DID routing to our server.
- Realtime bidirectional voice streaming.
- Toll-free/0800 numbers.
- Whether their “voice channels” are true live call channels or only automated voice-message capacity.
- Whether their PBX can hand calls to an external SIP URI/IP instead of only Termii’s own agent/contact-center product.

So, better answer: **Termii almost certainly has real voice/PBX-ish infrastructure, but public docs don’t prove it can replace Africa’s Talking for live Sabi calls yet.** The pricing makes it look promising; the developer docs still describe voice mostly as automated TTS/OTP-style calls.

For Sabi, ask them this exact thing:

> Can a Nigerian DID on Termii route inbound calls directly to our SIP/Asterisk PBX at a public IP, and can we place outbound calls from that PBX/API for live two-way AI tutoring? We need realtime conversational calls, not OTP voice or one-way text-to-speech alerts.

## Codex · 2026-06-17T20:56:56.929Z · final_answer

For our current Africa’s Talking SIP trunk:

**Provider-side likely limit:** Africa’s Talking’s public voice doc says they encourage up to **40 concurrent calls** for quality, and they “release one call per second.” Source: [Africa’s Talking concurrent calls help doc](https://help.africastalking.com/en/articles/1205758-how-many-concurrent-calls-can-i-make-per-second)

**Our PBX-side limit:** I checked the live Asterisk config. We have **no max call cap set**:
- `Maximum calls: Not set`
- Africa’s Talking endpoint shows `0 of inf`
- No `call-limit` / channel cap in our PJSIP config

So the practical answer is:

**The trunk can probably handle up to ~40 concurrent calls from AT’s side, unless they provisioned a lower cap specifically for our Nigeria DID/SIP trunk. Our server is not currently limiting it.**

But for Sabi quality, the real bottleneck is not SIP. It is the AI pipeline: Whisper STT + LLM + TTS per active call. I would trust **1-5 simultaneous premium tutoring calls today**, then load-test before promising 40 live AI conversations.

We should ask AT one exact question: “What concurrent call/channel limit is currently provisioned for DID `+2342017001459` on SIP trunk `136.243.8.51`?”

## Codex · 2026-06-18T14:03:34.803Z · final_answer

Yes. I’d treat the whole Codex universe like one portfolio, with **Sabi/Education for Equality as the flagship**, and everything else either supporting your operating system, public proof, or long-term life infrastructure.

Assuming “infinite time” means focused sequential work, not rushing, I’d stack it like this:

| Order | Project Lane | Finish Definition | Time | Cumulative |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | **Workspace Reset** | Clear disk, centralize secrets, list all deploy URLs, unblock Supabase/Xcode/Gmail accounts | 2-3 days | Day 3 |
| 1 | **Sabi Phone + Voice UX** | Nigerian number reliably works, inbound/callback policy settled, trunk capacity known, TTS voice chosen, logs/monitoring/load test ready | 1-2 weeks | Week 2 |
| 2 | **Sabi Curriculum + Validation** | Finish standards crosswalk, export assessment blueprints, create review queue, clean voice tags, prepare educator review packet | 2-3 weeks | Week 5 |
| 3 | **Sabi Pilot/Funding Package** | AIVA/demo-ready, reviewer plan, EduEvidence or equivalent path, AT/PressOne/Termii decision, outreach emails/advisors/contracts | 1-2 weeks | Week 7 |
| 4 | **Cortex + Sage + Kai** | Personal OS works: Cortex deployed with Supabase restored, Sage connected to all Gmail accounts, Kai calendar/music/focus flow stable | 4-6 weeks | Week 13 |
| 5 | **Go + Sleep Well** | Go database fixed and iPhone app usable; Sleep Well installed across devices with Screen Time/provisioning solved | 3-4 weeks | Week 17 |
| 6 | **Bethel / Knowledge System** | Journals, dreams, faith notes, memory, Sage/Cortex, and Remarkable/iCloud ingestion organized into one durable system | 4-8 weeks | Week 25 |
| 7 | **Creator Stack: Ed.it + Media** | Ed.it productionized, disk/render pipeline stable, real clips tested, content workflow tied to portfolio/social proof | 2-3 weeks | Week 28 |
| 8 | **Public Proof / Portfolio** | GitHub pins, portfolio, Dactyl, Adjutant, Rings, Index, Kai, Ed.it, Sage all cleanly presented | 1 week | Week 29 |
| 9 | **Long-Tail Admin** | Trademark/Ore, passport, advisor contracts, hackathons, fellowships, delegation system cleaned up | 2-4 weeks | Week 33 |

My strong recommendation: **do not spread your attention evenly.** The correct order is:

1. **Finish Sabi until it can survive real children calling it.**
2. **Formalize curriculum enough that serious educators can review it.**
3. **Package the mission for funding and partners.**
4. **Then finish your personal operating system tools: Cortex, Sage, Kai.**
5. **Then polish the auxiliary apps and public proof.**

The reason: Sabi is the only project with all four forces at once: mission, urgency, external partners, potential funding, and actual users. Kai, Cortex, Sage, Sleep Well, Go, Ed.it, and Bethel are powerful, but they either support Naomi-the-builder or Naomi-the-founder. Sabi is the thing most likely to become the center of gravity.

If I were turning this into your immediate execution plan, I’d start with:

1. Clear disk and unblock credentials.
2. Finish Sabi phone reliability and provider/capacity decision.
3. Finish Sabi curriculum validation packet.
4. Resume Cortex/Sage/Kai once Sabi is no longer fragile.
5. Use Ed.it/portfolio/GitHub as proof machinery after the core work is real.

Total realistic sequential build time: **about 7-8 months** to bring the whole ecosystem to a strong, coherent state. Sabi alone can be **pilot-ready much sooner: roughly 3-6 weeks** if it stays the top priority.

No, not **8 months of nonstop coding**. That was my “everything fully matured, externally validated, polished, documented, and de-risked” estimate.

If you coded intensely every day, starting from where things are now, I’d revise it like this:

**Sabi pilot-ready:** 10-21 days
Phone reliability, voice UX, trunk/provider decision, logs, basic load test, curriculum cleanup, demo path.

**Sabi educator/investor-ready:** 3-6 weeks
Standards mapping, review packet, validation plan, pitch/demo, external reviewers in motion.

**Cortex + Sage + Kai usable personal OS:** 2-4 weeks
Mostly credential/deploy cleanup plus product polish. The codebase already has a lot.

**Go + Sleep Well usable:** 1-2 weeks
Mostly Supabase/Xcode/provisioning/device blockers, not deep invention.

**Ed.it + portfolio/public proof:** 1-2 weeks
Already close. Needs disk, real examples, packaging.

**Bethel/deeper knowledge system:** 3-8 weeks
This depends on how spiritually/philosophically complete you want it. A useful v1 is much faster than the full cathedral version.

So the real answer is:

**If you go hard:**
- **3 weeks:** Sabi can be genuinely pilotable.
- **6 weeks:** Sabi can be serious enough for funders/educators.
- **10-12 weeks:** Most of your active projects can be usable and coherent.
- **3-4 months:** The whole ecosystem can feel polished, intentional, and not duct-taped together.

The longest thing is not raw coding. It is decisions, credentials, third-party providers, curriculum validation, Apple/Supabase weirdness, and making things feel premium instead of merely functional.

## Codex · 2026-06-18T14:48:12.482Z · final_answer

Less than “build Sabi,” more like **make Sabi trustworthy enough for real children**.

What’s left breaks into 6 lanes:

1. **Phone Reliability**
   Confirm the final phone path: Africa’s Talking vs PressOne/Termii fallback, direct inbound vs flash-callback, concurrent call limit, provider behavior for MTN/Glo/Airtel/9mobile/international callers, and call cost caps. Also add better call logs/monitoring so we can see every failed turn.

2. **Conversation Quality**
   Make Sabi feel premium: lower response latency, keep interruption/barge-in sharp, remove beeps if possible, stop her from saying `[laugh]`, “chuckle,” etc., fix “I didn’t catch that” loops, improve recognition of things like “50 naira,” and choose the final voice.

3. **Curriculum Completion**
   Finish the standards work properly: exact NERDC/Cambridge/GPF mapping, export the assessment blueprints, finish/verify any module the diagnostic can route a child into, clean all curriculum scripts of stage directions, and create a review queue for educators.

4. **Learning Memory + Placement**
   Make sure Sabi remembers where each child is, resumes correctly, places them into the right module, tracks mistakes, repeats concepts intelligently, and does not advance children too quickly.

5. **Pilot Safety + Ops**
   Add child-safety guardrails, abuse/rate limits, PII/transcript handling, parent/guardian consent language, call spending limits, failure fallbacks, and a simple admin view of calls/progress.

6. **Validation + Launch Package**
   Prepare the educator review packet, get reviewers, maybe EduEvidence or similar, write the pilot protocol, define success metrics, and package the demo for AIVA/funders/partners.

The **minimum pilot-ready Sabi** is probably:

- phone calls reliably connect,
- Sabi can hold a full lesson,
- she understands enough Nigerian/child speech to not frustrate users,
- the curriculum path is not broken,
- logs/costs/safety are visible,
- and you can show evidence that the curriculum is standards-aligned.

That is why I said **10-21 days for a serious pilot version** if we focus hard. The longer estimate was for Sabi becoming polished, validated, scalable, documented, and partner-ready.

## Codex · 2026-06-18T15:06:19.403Z · commentary

## Codex · 2026-06-18T15:06:23.176Z · final_answer

Not always.

If the call **reaches our PBX/SIP trunk**, yes, it should register somewhere on our side: Asterisk logs, CDR, maybe a recording file if it got far enough.

If the call reaches **Africa’s Talking but not our PBX**, it may show in the AT dashboard as a 0s/failed/success session depending on how far AT got.

If the call fails **before Africa’s Talking receives it**, like the caller’s carrier says “number does not exist,” bad international routing, MTN not routing the DID, Rebtel/Yolla weirdness, etc., then **our PBX will not see anything** and AT may also show nothing.

So for your mom’s MTN “number doesn’t exist” case: if MTN never handed the call to AT/upstream, it would not appear in our PBX logs. The Glo call worked because it actually routed through to us.

## Codex · 2026-06-18T15:15:25.062Z · final_answer

Yes. The clearest pattern from Viamo, DoorDash, Grubhub, ConnectEd, Rori, and the Edo AI pilot is:

**they did not validate by building the whole scaled machine first.** They validated with a painfully small real workflow, watched what broke, measured repeat behavior, then used those numbers to earn partners.

**What The Precedents Say**
DoorDash started as almost exactly the kind of “fake the system manually” model Sabi should use: a quick site with PDF menus and a Google Voice number. The founders personally took the first order, called the restaurant, delivered it, and kept doing deliveries every day for months before the real logistics platform existed. [Wired](https://www.wired.com/2015/11/doordash-wants-to-own-the-last-mile/) and DoorDash’s own S-1 both show the move: manual validation first, then marketplace scale to 390k+ merchants, 18M+ consumers, and 1M+ Dashers by 2020. [DoorDash S-1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1792789/000119312520292381/d752207ds1.htm)

Grubhub’s early moat was not fancy tech either. They solved a real analog mess: paper menus, phone-order errors, no delivery visibility. They literally called every restaurant in Chicago to build their data. By 2006 they had 75,000 monthly users, 30% monthly growth, and $2M in delivery orders; by IPO they had 3.4M active diners, 28,800 restaurants, and $1.3B gross food sales. [Grubhub early archive](https://about.grubhub.com/news/page/49/) / [Grubhub S-1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1594109/000119312514075544/d647121ds1.htm)

Viamo is the closest Sabi analog. Their 3-2-1 model proves basic-phone voice can scale: UNDP reports 35M+ users, 3M+ monthly active users, 81% repeat users, and 100M+ listening minutes/month. [UNDP Digital X](https://digitalx.undp.org/viamo-3-2-1-platform_1.html) Their Nigeria/Airtel 4-2-1 work also shows the partnership path: Airtel provided up to 10 free calls/month, Viamo handled platform + dashboard, content was translated, pretested, recorded, and monitored. [Breakthrough ACTION PDF](https://breakthroughactionandresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Partnering-with-the-Private-Sector-for-Mobile-Messaging.pdf)

Viamo’s AVA AI pilot is the future version of Sabi’s phone layer: basic voice calls + AI + localized approved info + manual safety review. Public data says AVA moved from prerecorded IVR into real voice AI, with pilots/rollout including Zambia, Nigeria, Tanzania, India, and Pakistan; Viamo manually reviews responses daily for sensitive topics. [BusinessWire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240315519318/en/Ask-Viamo-Anything-Combines-AI-with-Basic-Mobile-Calls-to-Bring-Next-Billion-Online) Stanford’s health AI whitepaper says the Zambia pilot reached ~32,000 users and 570,000 questions. [Stanford PDF](https://cdh.stanford.edu/sites/g/files/sbiybj29486/files/media/file/stanford_scdh_genaiwhitepaper_v18_compressed.pdf)

For learning validation, ConnectEd is the strongest phone precedent: one 20-minute call/week plus SMS for 8 weeks, TaRL-style targeting, 16,936 households across five countries, and 0.33 SD average learning gains. [J-PAL](https://www.povertyactionlab.org/blog/5-8-23/20-20-tutor-calling-targeted-instruction-phone-boosts-learning-across-six-countries) Rori proves AI tutoring can move math in Africa: ~1,000 students, 11 schools, two 30-minute sessions/week for 8 months, 0.37 SD effect. [Rori paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09809) The Edo/World Bank AI pilot shows the Nigeria-specific upside: 6 weeks, teacher-supported GPT-4/Copilot tutoring, ~0.3 SD gains, nearly two years of typical learning in six weeks. [World Bank](https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/education/From-chalkboards-to-chatbots-Transforming-learning-in-Nigeria)

**What This Means For Sabi**
The right plan is not “finish everything, then test.” It is:

1. Run a concierge phone pilot with 10-20 children.
   Use the current PBX. Monitor every call transcript. Let humans intervene behind the scenes. The metric is not “does the architecture scale?” It is: do children understand Sabi, answer, enjoy it, and call again?

2. Measure repeat behavior brutally.
   Track: first-call completion, second call within 72h, calls/week, lesson completion, “I didn’t catch that” rate, latency, dropout point, and parent/child comments.

3. Validate learning with a tiny TaRL-style design.
   Baseline diagnostic, 2-3 weeks of calls, endline diagnostic. Even 20 kids can reveal whether placement, pacing, voice quality, and remediation work before we spend pilot money.

4. Turn the 20-child pilot into a reviewer packet.
   Show call recordings, transcripts, learning movement, curriculum map, safety notes, and cost/minute. This is what we give educators, TaRL people, AT/PressOne/Termii, and funders.

5. Then run the serious pilot.
   100-300 children, 6 weeks, ideally delayed-start control. Target success bar: 0.25-0.35 SD or clear TaRL level movement, >50% weekly retention, stable phone connection across MTN/Glo/Airtel/9mobile, and cost per active learner.

My take: Sabi should copy DoorDash’s scrappiness, Viamo’s telco/content discipline, and ConnectEd/Rori’s evidence discipline. Tiny real calls first. Then proof. Then partner leverage.

## Codex · 2026-06-18T17:46:52.250Z · final_answer

Not sending yet. Here’s the plan and what Sonia needs.

**Plan**
We are asking Sonia to help turn Sabi’s first 10-child test from “kids try the phone” into a real educator-observed pre-pilot.

The flow is:

1. Recruit 10 children with caregiver consent.
2. Do a short baseline diagnostic: counting, simple operations, oral literacy/listening.
3. Let each child use Sabi over phone calls for 7-14 days.
4. Review every first call like educators would: did the child understand, respond, learn, stay engaged, get confused, need help?
5. Track repeat use: did the child come back for a second call within 72 hours?
6. Do a short endline check.
7. Sonia helps decide: greenlight 30-child micro-pilot, rerun another 10-child cycle, or pause and fix.

**What Sonia Needs**
She needs:

- The 10-child pre-pilot plan/runbook.
- The Sabi curriculum validation packet.
- The baseline/endline diagnostic questions.
- A lesson quality rubric: teachability, age fit, assessment validity, Nigerian context, safety.
- Access to call transcripts/summaries from the dashboard.
- A simple way to mark each call: strong, usable, weak, failed.
- The child/caregiver consent script.
- The list of 10 children, ages, network, language profile, and preferred call times.
- A weekly review rhythm: maybe 30-45 minutes every few days during the pre-pilot.

**Who Else She Needs**
Sonia should not carry the whole validation alone. She needs:

- A primary numeracy reviewer: to check counting, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, word problems.
- A foundational literacy/phonics reviewer: to check whether the oral literacy path is pedagogically real.
- A TaRL/assessment person: to check diagnostic placement and movement between levels.
- A field coordinator/caregiver liaison: to schedule children, get consent, handle parent questions.
- A technical operator: me/you/another Codex workflow watching call logs, dashboard, phone failures.
- Eventually, an external reviewer: TEP Centre, TaRL Africa, NERDC-adjacent educator, Cambridge consultant, or assessment specialist.

**Draft Email**
Subject: Educator review plan for Sabi’s first 10-child pre-pilot

Mum,

I wanted to share the educator-facing plan for Sabi’s first 10-child pre-pilot and ask for your help shaping it from the education side.

The goal is not to “scale” yet. The goal is to test Sabi carefully with 10 real children for 7-14 days and understand whether the phone experience can genuinely teach, not just technically work.

The plan is:

1. Recruit 10 children with caregiver consent and child assent.
2. Do a short baseline diagnostic in foundational numeracy and oral literacy.
3. Let each child use Sabi over phone calls.
4. Review every first call for clarity, engagement, age appropriateness, learning signal, and safety.
5. Track whether children return for a second call within 72 hours.
6. Do a short endline check.
7. Use the results to decide whether we are ready for a 30-child micro-pilot, or whether we need another 10-child cycle after fixes.

What I would really value from you is the educator lens: whether the diagnostic is fair, whether the lessons are teachable by voice, whether the children are responding naturally, and whether Sabi’s remediation actually helps when a child is confused.

For the plan to work, I think we will need:

- the 10-child roster with ages, phone networks, language profile, and preferred call times
- caregiver consent and child assent scripts
- baseline and endline diagnostic questions
- a simple educator rubric for reviewing calls
- reviewed call transcripts/summaries from the Sabi dashboard
- notes on what should change before we test with more children

I also do not think you should have to carry the whole review alone. We will likely need a numeracy reviewer, a foundational literacy/phonics reviewer, a TaRL or assessment person, and someone helping with caregiver scheduling and follow-up. Your role would be the lead educator/field reviewer: helping us make sure the pilot is realistic for Nigerian children and credible enough to show other educators.

Could you look over this plan and tell me what feels missing from an educator’s perspective? I especially want your view on what a child should be able to do before and after the 7-14 day test, and what would convince you that Sabi is actually teaching.

Love,
Naomi

## Codex · 2026-06-19T16:56:34.722Z · final_answer

It *can* be like that. The main reason it isn’t yet is probably not “Sabi is dumb”; it’s the STT pipeline around the model.

Dactly likely feels perfect because it is getting cleaner audio and/or doing better endpointing: continuous mic audio, better noise handling, less clipping at the start/end of speech, and maybe a better STT provider for short phrases.

Our phone path is harder:

- Phone audio is narrowband PSTN audio, usually 8kHz mono, much worse than browser mic audio.
- Our Asterisk loop has to decide when you started/stopped talking. If that timing is off, it clips “Naomi” or “fifty naira” before STT even sees the full word.
- Whisper/Groq is okay, but short answers and names are exactly where generic STT can be weird.
- We are not yet using per-question expected-answer hints deeply enough, like “the child will probably say 50 naira / fifty naira / ₦50.”

So the move is: don’t just swap TTS voices. We need to make STT more like Dactly by improving capture + recognition together.

The strongest fix path:

1. Stop treating “name” and “math answer” like open-ended dictation.
2. For each turn, pass expected answer hints into STT/grading.
3. Add phonetic/number normalization before marking wrong.
4. For phone calls, loosen and stabilize endpointing so we don’t clip the first syllable.
5. If Dactly has an API or you can tell me what STT provider it uses, we can test swapping Sabi to that directly.

For the “50 naira but Sabi said wrong” case, I’m almost certain we need to fix answer matching, not just STT. If STT hears “fifty naira,” Sabi should accept `50`, `₦50`, `fifty`, `fifty naira`, “50 naira,” and common mishears.

## Codex · 2026-06-19T19:47:31.314Z · final_answer

Yes, we can use YarnGPT, but not as the default live phone voice yet.

I checked the live call. Production was set to:

`SABI_TTS_PRIMARY=yarngpt`
`SABI_YARNGPT_VOICE=wura`

So YarnGPT was using **Wura**.

Why it switched voices: the code was trying YarnGPT first. When YarnGPT worked, you heard Wura. When YarnGPT timed out, it fell back to ElevenLabs, so the next Sabi response sounded like a different person. In the live call, YarnGPT took about **2.6-5s** on successful turns and timed out on longer turns, then ElevenLabs took over. That is why it felt inconsistent.

I switched production back to **ElevenLabs-primary** now:

`SABI_TTS_PRIMARY=elevenlabs`

The YarnGPT component will still initialize, so logs may say `YarnGPT TTS ready (voice=Wura)`, but it is no longer the primary voice for live calls.

Testing plan before using YarnGPT live:
1. Generate 50-100 common Sabi lines with YarnGPT Wura offline.
2. Measure latency, failure rate, and audio consistency.
3. Pre-cache fixed lines: greeting, retry prompts, “well done,” “say that again,” transition lines.
4. Add a per-call voice lock so one call never flips between YarnGPT and ElevenLabs.
5. Test 5-10 calls with YarnGPT behind a flag.
6. Only switch default if p95 TTS time is low enough and timeouts are rare.

You can call again now; it should be ElevenLabs and should not switch voices.

## Codex · 2026-06-19T20:33:29.822Z · final_answer

We got the server because the Africa’s Talking path needed a real SIP/PBX endpoint, not just a normal web callback.

In plain terms:

- Africa’s Talking could do the old HTTPS `<Play><Record>` flow, but that could not do real back-and-forth interruption.
- For a premium “talk over Sabi and she stops” experience, we needed full-duplex audio.
- AT told us to route the DID to `trunk:136.243.8.51`, which means we needed a public server at that IP listening on SIP `UDP/5060` and RTP media ports.
- That server runs Asterisk/PBX plus the Sabi realtime voice stack.
- It also lets us inspect SIP logs, call recordings, audio directions, STT, TTS, and timing directly, which is how we’ve been debugging the phone.

So the server is basically Sabi’s phone brain and switchboard: AT sends calls there, Asterisk answers, then our Python voice agent handles STT, LLM, TTS, interruption, logs, and recordings.

## Codex · 2026-06-22T17:20:22.717Z · final_answer

I checked without changing anything.

**What I see**
No phone calls reached our PBX in the last ~3 hours today, June 22. The live server only shows health checks and blocked web scanner traffic. The newest call recordings on the PBX are from **June 20**, not today. So if someone just got “timed out” or “call cannot be completed,” that likely happened before the call reached our server: AT/carrier routing, MTN/Glo/Airtel path, or the caller app/network.

**Why Sabi feels less comprehensive**
Yes, I see why. The recent phone-code changes made Sabi more “fast phone convo” than “rich lesson”:

- LLM max output was reduced from `200` tokens to `90`.
- Prompt now says ordinary replies should be under `12 spoken words`.
- The phone path still does **not** load the actual 5-7 minute lesson scripts.
- It has an 8-minute cap, but it does not enforce a complete 5-7 minute lesson arc.

So Sabi is currently a short adaptive tutor, not yet the full hackathon-style lesson runner.

**STT**
Current production STT is Groq Whisper. I agree we should test Nigeria-specific/accent-robust options before switching. Existing plan already names a bakeoff: Groq Whisper, OpenAI `gpt-4o-transcribe`, Deepgram Nova-3/Flux, Speechmatics Global English, and AfriSpeech/Intron-style African-accent routes.

Useful source notes: OpenAI’s transcription models support prompts/logprobs for `gpt-4o-transcribe` ([docs](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/speech-to-text)); Deepgram Nova-3 supports keyterm prompting ([docs](https://developers.deepgram.com/docs/keyterm)); AfriSpeech is a Pan-African accented English ASR dataset ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.00274)).

**Charging / toll-free**
Do not assume it is toll-free. `+2342017001459` is not obviously a toll-free number. If 3 users were not charged, it may be their bundle/free minutes, delayed balance updates, or carrier-specific behavior. Our AT wallet charges are our side; the caller’s airtime charge is controlled by their carrier unless AT explicitly confirms toll-free/reverse billing.

**Can we know children are calling?**
Not from caller ID alone. Best way is a pre-pilot roster: parent/guardian phone number, child first name or nickname, age band, school/community, consent status, then Sabi asks at start: “Is the learner with you now?” We can log call duration, transcript, phone number, and learner profile, but we should not pretend voice alone proves it is a child.

## Codex · 2026-06-22T19:32:59.282Z · final_answer

Made another concrete step toward the full phone-line goal and deployed it to the PBX.

**Changed**
- Added an explicit TaRL-style diagnostic router in [diagnostic_flow.py](</Users/naomiivie/Education for Equality/sabi-server/diagnostic_flow.py>).
- Wired it into [llm.py](</Users/naomiivie/Education for Equality/sabi-server/llm.py>) so Sabi now gets a hard instruction for the next baseline step: ask the next diagnostic item, stop after a miss, place the child, then begin a mini-lesson.
- Updated [learning_state.py](</Users/naomiivie/Education for Equality/sabi-server/learning_state.py>) so diagnostic misses produce real placement fields: module, week, lesson, TaRL level, and reason.
- Fixed the realtime call opening in [voice_realtime.py](</Users/naomiivie/Education for Equality/sabi-server/voice_realtime.py>): Sabi now looks up the caller before greeting, so returning children are not asked their name again before memory loads.
- Mirrored that in [voice_asterisk.py](</Users/naomiivie/Education for Equality/sabi-server/voice_asterisk.py>).

I anchored the diagnostic design to TaRL’s official principles: quick oral one-on-one assessment, contextual items, progressive up/down placement, and teaching from the child’s actual level. I also cross-checked against Cambridge Primary’s progression/assessment framing and CAST UDL assessment guidance for frequent formative checks and reducing assessment barriers:
[TaRL Assessment](https://teachingattherightlevel.org/the-tarl-approach/assessment/), [Cambridge Primary Mathematics](https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/programmes-and-qualifications/cambridge-primary/curriculum/mathematics/), [CAST UDL Assessment Tips](https://www.cast.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/cast-udltipsforassessment-20200920-a11y.pdf).

**Verified**
- Local Python compile passed.
- Local `learning_state_regression.py` passed.
- Local `stt_regression.py`: `9/9 passed`.
- `curriculum-app` build passed.
- Deployed to `136.243.8.51`.
- Production health OK.
- Production `learning_state_regression.py` passed.
- Production `stt_regression.py`: `9/9 passed`.
- Phone duplicates check: `PHONE_ROWS=33 DUPES={}`.

**Still Open**
The big remaining blocker is Supabase schema: live Supabase still does not have `phone_number_normalized`, `learning_state`, `current_module`, `baseline_status`, etc. The code has fallbacks and can infer from saved session messages, but truly durable “continue exactly from where the child stopped” needs the migration in [supabase-sabi-learning-state.sql](</Users/naomiivie/Education for Equality/curriculum-app/supabase-sabi-learning-state.sql>) applied in Supabase.

## Codex · 2026-06-22T19:37:35.560Z · final_answer

I tightened the continuation layer and deployed it.

The important change: because live Supabase is still on the thin schema, Sabi now reconstructs learner state by replaying up to 20 previous session transcripts oldest-to-newest, instead of only looking at the latest session. That means if a child was placed in Module 1 during an earlier diagnostic and then had another call later, Sabi can still infer “continue Module 1 counting” even before the richer `learning_state` columns exist.

I also fixed name capture so junk STT like “thank you,” “and some,” or “numerous” does not get saved as a child’s name just because it came after “what is your name?”

Verified on production:
- Health OK
- STT regression: `9/9 passed`
- Learning-state regression: passed, including:
  - returning caller not asked for name again
  - diagnostic miss places at module/week/lesson
  - old sessions replay into the correct continuation state
  - non-name phrases rejected
- Live reconstruction sample now gives coherent states like:
  - `+18604367048`: module 1, guided practice, diagnostic done
  - `+2348033374126`: module 1, guided practice, diagnostic done
  - `+2347054987372`: module 2, first mini lesson, diagnostic done

Still not full completion of the big goal: Supabase still needs the richer schema migration applied for first-class durable state columns. But the live server is now much more robust even before that migration.

## Codex · 2026-06-22T19:53:22.883Z · final_answer

No, the short cutoffs are not supposed to be normal. The live Sabi limit is `480s` / 8 minutes, so a 5-7 minute lesson should fit. The latest ~3 minute call ended because I restarted the `sabi-server` container during deployment, which killed the active AudioSocket stream. Separately, I found one real early-ending bug: Sabi could hang up if she said “see you next time” or “talk to you” too early. I fixed that in [voice_asterisk.py](/Users/naomiivie/Education%20for%20Equality/sabi-server/voice_asterisk.py), deployed it, and verified live: early closing phrases no longer end the call before 10 user turns, but an actual caller “bye” still ends it.

On the toll-free thing: we are **not** truly toll-free. This is still the AT Nigerian DID `+2342017001459` routed to our SIP trunk, not an 0800/toll-free/zero-rated number. If callers say they weren’t charged, that may be their bundle/free minutes/network behavior, or the charge may not show immediately. AT is definitely still billing our wallet for answered inbound/SIP minutes. “Basic” is just the AT billing tier/balance band, not “free.” AT’s voice docs distinguish regular, toll-free, and SIP trunking products, and our current setup is SIP/regular DID, not toll-free: [Africa’s Talking Voice](https://africastalking.com/voice), [Pricing](https://africastalking.com/pricing).

So: test again now. If it cuts around 8 minutes, that is our cap. If it cuts around 1-3 minutes again, that is still a bug/provider drop and I’ll trace the exact call log.

## Codex · 2026-06-22T21:29:16.591Z · final_answer

Yes. For **testing Sabi in Lagos now**, I’d use a small trusted field partner first, not government first.

**Best first targets**
1. **The Destiny Trust / OurSchool**
Best fit. They already work with vulnerable children in Lagos and run digital/offline learning spaces. This is probably the cleanest “put Sabi in front of 10 children safely” partner.
Contact page: [ourschool.africa/contact](https://www.ourschool.africa/contact)

2. **Ovie Brume Foundation**
Good controlled environment: youth centre, free educational/social programmes for underserved children in Surulere. Easier than a huge NGO.
Source/contact: [oviebrumefoundation.org](https://oviebrumefoundation.org/)

3. **Slum2School Africa**
Very strong mission fit and Lagos-based, but probably more formal/bigger. Good for a 25-100 child pilot after the 10-child test.
Source: [slum2school.org](https://slum2school.org/)

4. **LOTS Charity Foundation, Ajegunle/Dustbin Estate**
Very ground-level, underserved-community fit. Might be less formal but very useful for real-world testing if you have a trusted intro.
Source: [LOTS Charity Foundation X](https://x.com/LotsCharityNG)

5. **Teach For Nigeria fellows/alumni**
Best if you want a teacher-supervised school test. They have fellows across Nigeria and have worked in Lagos/Ogun schools.
Source: [teachfornigeria.org](https://teachfornigeria.org/)

6. **Chess in Slums Africa**
Good audience and strong child engagement culture. Better for “will kids love this and return?” than for formal assessment.
Source: [chessinslumsafrica.com](https://chessinslumsafrica.com/)

**For credibility/assessment, not first distribution**
- **TEP Centre / LEARNigeria**: best for validating Sabi’s baseline and learning measurement. LEARNigeria focuses on foundational literacy/numeracy assessment in Nigeria.
Sources: [LEARNigeria](https://learnigeria.org/), [TEP Centre LEARNigeria](https://tepcentre.com/learnigeria/)
- **LASUBEB/EKOEXCEL**: important later, but not the fastest first test. EKOEXCEL covers about 500,000 pupils across 1,016 Lagos public primary schools, so it’s a scale route after you have evidence.
Source: [LASUBEB EKOEXCEL](https://lasubeb.lg.gov.ng/lasubeb-ekoexcel)

**If you mean literal dropshipping materials**
Use a Lagos printer + courier:
- Flyers/cards: Printrush Naija or Hazken
- Same-day Lagos delivery: Kwik
- More structured courier: GIG Logistics

My recommendation: **start with The Destiny Trust, Ovie Brume, and one Teach For Nigeria/Lagos teacher contact in parallel**. Ask for only: “10 children, 7 days, caregiver consent, supervised phone calls, short feedback form.” That’s small enough to get a yes.

## Codex · 2026-06-22T21:51:03.663Z · final_answer

Made another concrete step toward the real end state: I proved and fixed live Supabase save/resume behavior.

What I found:
- Live `sabi_students` is still thin: no `current_module`, `learning_state`, `learner_key`, etc.
- Live `sabi_sessions` does have enough to support resume: `messages`, `call_sid`, `phone_number`, `channel`, duration, scores.

What broke:
- Sabi was saving the learning snapshot, and resume state did reconstruct correctly.
- But because `topics_covered`/`recommended_module` are missing, the fallback stripped all optional session columns, including existing ones like `call_sid` and `phone_number`. That made monitoring/debugging weaker.

What I fixed:
- Changed persistence fallback to remove only the specific missing optional columns, preserving live columns that do exist.
- Deployed to `136.243.8.51`.
- Commit pushed: `d1942a4 Preserve Sabi session audit columns on thin schema`.

Verified live:
- Fake student call saved to Supabase.
- Same phone returned the same student row.
- Session was retrievable by `call_sid`.
- One `SABI_LEARNING_STATE_SNAPSHOT` was saved.
- Resume reconstructed: `current_module=1`, `diagnostic_status=done`, `current_week=1`, `current_lesson=1`, `active_skill=counting`.
- Cleanup left zero test rows.
- Container regressions passed, STT regressions passed, health OK.

## Codex · 2026-06-22T21:55:25.570Z · final_answer

For **right now**, I would not “dropship” Sabi cold. I’d set up a tiny Lagos test cell:

1. **Sonia supervises**
   She is already your Lagos Regional Coordinator. Ask her to find one trusted field helper through her former EKOEXCEL/headteacher/community network.

2. **Hire one local field runner**
   Profile: former teacher, community mobilizer, NYSC education corps member, or NGO field officer near **Mushin / Ajeromi-Ifelodun**. Their job is to buy/receive phones, insert MTN/Glo/Airtel SIMs, test calls, deliver to caregivers, sit through first calls, log what happens.

3. **Best orgs to ask for referrals**
   - **SEED Care & Support Foundation**: strongest fit for low-cost schools / Lagos education ecosystem. They list Lagos school-network work and contact: `info@seedfoundation.ng`, `+2349020025605`. [SEED](https://seedfoundation.ng/)
   - **Slum2School Africa**: strong underserved-child education network in Lagos; good for volunteer/referral path, maybe slower institutionally. [Slum2School](https://slum2school.org/privacy/)
   - **Restore Foundation for Child Sight**: has done school work in **Mushin** and lists direct Lagos contacts. Useful for “who knows schools/community people in Mushin?” [Restore Foundation](https://restorefoundationng.org/training/)
   - **LASUBEB / Ajeromi-Ifelodun LGEA**: better for formal pilot access, not fastest scrappy testing. Official LASUBEB page lists Ajeromi-Ifelodun education contact details. [LASUBEB LGEA](https://lasubeb.lg.gov.ng/lasubeb-lg-education-authority)

4. **For actual delivery/logistics**
   Use logistics only after a human has set up the phones/SIMs:
   - [Gokada](https://www.gokada.ng/) for Lagos delivery
   - [Kwik](https://kwik.delivery/) for 2-hour Lagos delivery
   - [Dellyman](https://dellyman.com/) / [Peng Logistics](https://www.penglogistics.com/p/delivery-company-in-lagos.html) as backup

5. **For recruiting backup field staff**
   If warm referrals fail: post/search on [Jobberman NGO Lagos](https://www.jobberman.com/jobs/ngo-npo-charity/lagos), [MyJobMag NGO jobs](https://www.myjobmag.com/jobs-by-field/ngo), and LinkedIn field research jobs. But this is slower.

My strongest recommendation: **Sonia + one paid local runner + 10-child pre-pilot.** Pay the runner a short test stipend plus transport, maybe ₦50k-₦100k for a tightly scoped week, then move to a proper monthly coordinator if they’re excellent.

## Codex · 2026-06-22T22:13:05.738Z · final_answer

Yes. Best stack:

1. **Sonia as the anchor**
   She is already written into our pilot docs as Lagos Regional Coordinator for Mushin/Ajeromi-Ifelodun: recruit schools/cohorts, get parent consent, run TaRL assessments, handle materials, and send daily reports. So I’d dropship any test kit to her first.

2. **One adult Lagos telecom tester**
   For phone reliability only, not child testing. Ask them to test MTN, Glo, Airtel, 9mobile, noisy room, feature phone vs smartphone, inbound vs callback, and record: connect time, “can hear Sabi,” STT accuracy, cutoff time. Use existing registered SIMs because new Nigerian SIMs require NIN/VNIN registration per MTN’s SIM registration guidance.

3. **Teach For Nigeria**
   Good for teacher/fellow access and school-facing testing. Their model is already about placing fellows/leaders in underserved education contexts, and they mention a large fellow/alumni movement. [Teach For Nigeria](https://teachfornigeria.org/)

4. **Slum2School Africa**
   Strong fit for underserved/out-of-school child access, but use them for a proper partner pilot, not casual testing. They are Lagos-based and have “Volunteer” / “Become a Partner” paths. [Slum2School](https://slum2school.org/)

5. **Chess in Slums Africa**
   Very relevant for low-income child/community testing in Lagos. They publish contact details: `partnerships@chessinslumsafrica.com`, `hello@chessinslumsafrica.com`, WhatsApp `+234 810 337 9260`, office in Yaba. [Chess in Slums contact](https://chessinslumsafrica.com/contacts/)

6. **CcHUB / re:learn**
   Better for product/UX/advisory help than field child recruitment. They have Lagos presence in Yaba and list Education as a focus area. [CcHUB](https://cchub.africa/cchub-design-lab-rwanda-launched-the-product-experience-factory/product-experience/)

My recommendation: **today, use Sonia + one adult SIM/network tester. This week, move to Sonia + 2 trusted teachers/parents + 5-10 children with consent. In parallel, email Chess in Slums and Slum2School for a structured pilot.**

For the test kit: basic phone, cheap Android for recording/WhatsApp, power bank, airtime, test checklist, consent script, and SIM coverage across MTN/Glo/Airtel/9mobile.
