Yes. Fastest answer: **Sonia is your first node**, then she pulls one trusted local field assistant and 10 families through school/community relationships. For this week, don’t cold-recruit children online.

**Best Helpers**
1. **Dr. Sonia Ivie**
   Already formalized in your docs as Lagos Regional Coordinator. She should source the first 10 children, manage parent consent, and appoint one trusted field assistant near Mushin/Ajeromi.

2. **Your advisor network: Remi Tanimola, Rhoda Odigboh, Sonia’s former EKOEXCEL/NewGlobe contacts**
   Best for safe child access, headteacher referrals, and adults who understand Lagos public-school children.

3. **Slum2School Africa**
   Strong fit for underserved Lagos children and community-led education work. Good later partner, maybe not instant unless Sonia/board has a warm intro.
   [slum2school.org](https://slum2school.org/)

4. **Street Child Care & Welfare Initiative**
   Good fit for vulnerable/street-connected children and child-protection-aware testing. They list Lagos contact details publicly.
   [sccwi.org/contact-us](https://sccwi.org/contact-us/)

5. **Teach For Nigeria fellows/alumni**
   Good for finding young educators who can observe tests, help with baseline/endline, and supervise calls.
   [teachfornigeria.org](https://teachfornigeria.org/)

6. **CcHUB re:learn**
   Better for edtech/product validation, UX feedback, and possible credibility, not necessarily immediate child recruitment.
   [CcHUB re:learn](https://cchub.africa/impact/relearn/)

7. **Chess in Slums Africa**
   Possible later community partner for marginalized children, but I’d approach after you have a clean 10-child pilot protocol.
   [chessinslumsafrica.com](https://chessinslumsafrica.com/)

For **dropshipping/logistics**, use local buying/delivery rather than shipping from the US unless necessary:
- **Kwik** for same-day Lagos delivery. [kwik.delivery](https://kwik.delivery/)
- **GIG Logistics** for Nigeria-wide / US-to-Nigeria shipping. [giglogistics.com](https://giglogistics.com/)
- Buy phones/materials locally where possible; SIMs are messy because Nigerian SIM registration/NIN makes casual distribution annoying.

My recommendation: **Sonia + one trusted field assistant + 10 caregiver phones across MTN/Glo/Airtel/9mobile.** No new phones at first unless a child truly has no access. Your own pre-pilot plan already says 10 children, consent/assent, baseline, first-call review within 24h, and daily monitoring in `/sabi/prepilot`: [SABI_10_CHILD_PREPILOT_INFRASTRUCTURE_PLAN.md](</Users/naomiivie/Education for Equality/pilot/infrastructure/SABI_10_CHILD_PREPILOT_INFRASTRUCTURE_PLAN.md>).

## Codex · 2026-06-22T22:32:36.303Z · commentary

## Codex · 2026-06-22T22:33:30.982Z · final_answer

I wrote the research brief here: [SABI_END_OF_CALL_FEEDBACK_RESEARCH.md](/Users/naomiivie/Education%20for%20Equality/3.%20The%20Evidence/SABI_END_OF_CALL_FEEDBACK_RESEARCH.md).

Core finding: the best teams do not add a long “how was it?” survey. They capture feedback immediately after the call, keep it under 1-2 minutes, use 1-3 structured questions, then one short open-ended voice note. For Sabi, I’d do:

1. “Optional: leave a short recorded note to help us improve Sabi.”
2. Rating: “From 1 to 5, how clearly could you hear Sabi?”
3. Rating: “From 1 to 5, how well did Sabi understand the child?”
4. Voice note: “Tell us one thing that felt good, confusing, slow, or broken. You have 45 seconds.”

Important child-safety piece: for children, this should only happen in tester/pre-pilot mode with guardian consent and child assent. The child version should be much softer: “You can tell me one thing that was easy or hard, or you can say no.” No business/product jargon.

Sources I used include Verint and Talkdesk post-call IVR survey guidance, Qualtrics customer-feedback practice, Twilio/Africa’s Talking recording docs, DoorDash/Grubhub/UberEATS product-research writeups, IDinsight SMS/IVR survey lessons, UNICEF consultation guidance, HHS children-in-research guidance, and our existing Sabi safeguarding + validation files.

My recommendation: build this behind a flag first: `SABI_FEEDBACK_MODE=testers`, linked to `call_id`, with raw audio retained only short-term and redacted transcript/tags kept for product review.

## Codex · 2026-06-22T22:36:25.627Z · final_answer

Yes, I would reach out now, but softly.

Not: “Can CcHUB validate our product?”
Better: “Could re:learn/CcHUB advise us on how to structure a credible Lagos pre-pilot and what evidence they would want to see before we apply to future EdTech support programs?”

Why yes:
CcHUB’s re:learn is literally their education practice, focused on tech-enabled learning in Nigerian schools for ages 5-18. Their Mastercard Foundation EdTech Fellowship is built around inclusive, context-relevant edtech for underserved learners, and Cohort 4 emphasized implementation readiness, learning outcomes, mentorship, technical support, and ecosystem partners. That is extremely close to Sabi’s lane. Sources: [CcHUB re:learn](https://cchub.africa/impact/relearn/), [CcHUB education](https://cchub.africa/aof/education/), [Cohort 4 page](https://futureoflearning.cchub.africa/cohort-4/).

But timing matters:
Cohort 4 applications opened February 27, 2026 and closed April 10, 2026, so this is not about applying right this second. It is about relationship-building before the next window and getting credible validation structure. CcHUB said the fellowship has supported dozens of African edtech companies and is tied to evidence-based innovation and AI in learning, so a thoughtful early note is appropriate. Source: [CcHUB Cohort 4 announcement](https://cchub.africa/cohort-4-of-cchubs-edtech-fellowship-targets-early-stage-startups-innovating-for-the-underserved-learners/).

My recommendation:
Send a concise email after we have the phone line stable enough for a 5-minute demo and a one-page pre-pilot plan. If you want to send today, frame it as “we’re preparing a 10-child Lagos validation and would value advice,” not “please validate us.”

Ask for:
1. A 20-minute advisory call.
2. Feedback on the 10-child pre-pilot design.
3. What evidence CcHUB/re:learn would consider credible for a future fellowship/application.
4. Whether they know an educator/research reviewer who could sanity-check the pilot.

Do not overclaim yet. Say “working prototype,” “pre-pilot,” “seeking validation guidance,” and “phone-first AI tutor for foundational literacy/numeracy.” That sounds serious, not weird.

## Codex · 2026-06-22T23:34:08.391Z · commentary

## Codex · 2026-06-22T23:34:12.939Z · commentary

## Codex · 2026-06-22T23:34:18.823Z · commentary

## Codex · 2026-06-22T23:40:18.964Z · final_answer

The thing you’re thinking of may be called a **Terms of Reference** or a **Working Agreement / Team Charter**.

For you and Sonia, I’d use a living **Google Doc or Notion page** called:

**Sonia x Education for Equality Working Agreement**

Best structure:

1. **Purpose**
   What Sonia is helping E4E do.

2. **Scope of Work**
   Curriculum review, lesson feedback, learner assessment design, pilot planning, educator validation, etc.

3. **Expectations**
   What you need from her, how often, quality bar, response times, meeting rhythm.

4. **Deliverables**
   Example: review 5 lessons, suggest changes, help design feedback rubric, join pilot debrief.

5. **Decision Rights**
   What Sonia advises on vs. what you decide.

6. **Timeline**
   Week 1, Week 2, Week 3.

7. **Communication**
   WhatsApp for quick things, Google Doc comments for curriculum, weekly call for decisions.

8. **Credit / Compensation**
   Whether she is volunteer advisor, paid reviewer, credited educator, future curriculum lead, etc.

9. **Confidentiality**
   Keep child data, lesson materials, and pilot feedback private.

If this is informal, call it a **Working Agreement**. If you want it to sound more professional/nonprofit/education-sector, call it **Terms of Reference**. For Sonia, I’d probably use **Terms of Reference** because it feels educator-facing and serious without sounding too legal.

## Codex · 2026-06-22T23:41:50.949Z · final_answer

Yes. For **building an actual organization**, not just “being a founder,” I’d read these in this order:

1. **[The Great CEO Within](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ZJZbv4J6FZ8Dnb0JuMhJxTnwl-dwqx5xl0s65DE3wO8/mobilebasic) — Matt Mochary**
   Best first read. Extremely tactical: meetings, accountability, feedback, delegation, hiring, decision-making.

2. **[Scaling People](https://press.stripe.com/scaling-people) — Claire Hughes Johnson**
   Probably the most useful for E4E/Sabi next. It covers operating systems, hiring, management, foundational documents, performance, and culture.

3. **[High Output Management](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/72467/high-output-management-by-andrew-s-grove-former-chairman-and-ceo-of-intel/) — Andy Grove**
   The management classic. Best for learning how to make teams produce excellent work consistently.

4. **[Good Strategy/Bad Strategy](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/208668/good-strategy-bad-strategy-by-richard-rumelt/) — Richard Rumelt**
   Essential so E4E doesn’t become a pile of dreams, grants, features, and urgency. It teaches what a real strategy is.

5. **[The Effective Executive](https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-effective-executive-peter-f-drucker) — Peter Drucker**
   Best for you personally as CEO: what to focus on, how to make decisions, how not to drown in important work.

6. **[The Advantage](https://www.amazon.com/Advantage-Organizational-Health-Everything-Business/dp/0470941529) — Patrick Lencioni**
   Good for making the organization emotionally and operationally healthy: clarity, trust, meetings, alignment.

For you specifically, I’d start with **The Great CEO Within**, then **Scaling People**, then **Good Strategy/Bad Strategy**. That trio will help you build the actual operating backbone for Sabi and E4E.

---

# Parental Consent Form
## Sabi Voice Learning Pre-Pilot

**Education for Equality**

Dear Parent/Guardian,

Education for Equality is beginning a small pre-pilot of **Sabi**, a voice-based learning assistant that teaches children foundational literacy and numeracy through phone calls.

Sabi speaks with the child, asks simple questions, listens to the child’s answers, and gives patient step-by-step support. The goal is to help children practise reading, sounds, counting, addition, subtraction, and everyday problem-solving in a warm and encouraging way.

## Key Milestone Achieved

Sabi is now ready for early testing with children. The voice agent can run full short lessons, respond to children’s answers, teach patiently, and support learning over the phone. This pre-pilot will help us understand how well Sabi works for real children and what we need to improve before a larger pilot.

## Purpose of the Pre-Pilot

This pre-pilot will help us understand:

- Whether children can learn comfortably through phone calls.
- Whether Sabi explains lessons clearly.
- Whether children enjoy the learning experience.
- Whether parents find the programme useful.
- What should be improved before a larger launch.

## Duration

The pre-pilot is expected to run for **3 to 6 months**. Participation is voluntary, and parents may withdraw their child at any time.

## Mode of Delivery

Lessons will be delivered through **phone calls**. A child will either call into Sabi or receive a scheduled learning call, depending on the testing arrangement.

Each learning session will be short, usually around:

- **5 minutes of literacy**
- **5 minutes of numeracy**

No airtime top-ups or recharge cards will be given as part of this pilot. This is to avoid misuse and to keep the testing focused on learning outcomes.

## Times of Calling

The expected call times are:

- **Out-of-school / market children:** Morning sessions, between **8:00am and 12:00pm**
- **In-school children:** Evening sessions, after school and after they return home

Exact timing will be coordinated with parents/guardians.

## Parent/Guardian’s Role

Parents/guardians are asked to:

- Give permission for the child to participate.
- Help ensure the child is available at agreed call times.
- Provide a safe and quiet space where possible.
- Encourage the child, without answering for them.
- Tell the team if the child feels uncomfortable or wants to stop.
- Share feedback about the child’s experience.

## Child’s Role

The child will be asked to:

- Speak with Sabi during the phone lesson.
- Try their best to answer questions.
- Ask for help if they do not understand.
- Tell a parent/guardian if they do not want to continue.

## Call Recording and Feedback

Some calls may be recorded for learning review, quality improvement, safety, and feedback. These recordings help us understand whether Sabi is hearing children correctly, teaching clearly, and responding appropriately.

At the end of some calls, the child or tester may be invited to leave an optional voice note about the experience. This can include anything that felt good, confusing, uncomfortable, or worth improving.

Recordings and feedback will be handled carefully and used only for improving the programme.

## Voluntary Participation

Participation is completely voluntary. Refusing to participate will not affect the child’s schooling, church/community participation, or relationship with Education for Equality.

Parents/guardians may withdraw consent at any time by contacting the project team.

## Expected Benefits

Your child may benefit from:

- Extra practice in literacy and numeracy.
- More confidence speaking and answering questions.
- Personalised support at their current learning level.
- Short, accessible lessons without needing internet or a smartphone.

This is still a pilot, so we cannot guarantee specific academic improvement for every child.

## Possible Risks or Discomforts

The risks are minimal, but a child may sometimes feel shy, confused, or tired during a call. If this happens, the child may stop, and the parent/guardian may contact the team.

## Consent Statement

[  ] I understand that my child’s participation is voluntary.

## Codex · 2026-06-23T19:48:06.956Z · final_answer

I checked the research. Recommendation: **do not merge literacy + numeracy into one long lesson**. Keep them as **two short lessons**. Best learning design is:

- Ideal: one 5-7 minute literacy call and one 5-7 minute numeracy call at different points in the day.
- Practical pilot option: if the family only has one phone window, do them back-to-back **with a 2-3 minute break**.
- Do not make one continuous 12-15 minute call. Our own Sabi voice lesson design says audio-only learning should stay 5-7 minutes, one concept per call, with questions every 30-60 seconds. Research on spacing/retrieval also supports spreading learning across lessons instead of cramming everything into one session.

Sources I checked: [Sabi Voice Lesson Design](/Users/naomiivie/Education%20for%20Equality/2.%20The%20Solution/SABI_VOICE_LESSON_DESIGN.md), [IES Practice Guide on spacing/quizzing](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/Docs/PracticeGuide/20072004.pdf), [AERO spacing and retrieval guide](https://www.edresearch.edu.au/guides-resources/practice-guides/spacing-and-retrieval-practice-guide-full-publication), [UNICEF consent/assent guidance](https://www.unicef.org/youthledaction/media/791/file/UNICEF-Guidance-on-Consultations-with-Young-People.pdf.pdf).

Here is the revised form.

---

# Parental Consent Form
## Sabi Voice Learning Pre-Pilot

**Education for Equality**

Dear Parent/Guardian,

Education for Equality is beginning a small pre-pilot of **Sabi**, an AI voice learning agent that teaches children how to read, write, and do basic mathematics through phone calls.

Sabi speaks with the child, asks simple questions, listens to the child’s answers, and gives patient step-by-step support. We are doing this pre-pilot to test the product, understand how children learn with Sabi, and improve it for future versions.

## What Sabi Is

Sabi is an AI voice tutor. Your child will speak with Sabi on the phone for short lessons. Sabi will help your child practise foundational literacy and numeracy, including letter sounds, simple words, reading, counting, addition, subtraction, and everyday money problems.

## Key Learning Milestone

The goal of this pre-pilot is for each child to make clear progress toward:

- Learning how to read and write.
- Reading simple words and short sentences with more confidence.
- Counting, adding, subtracting, and solving basic maths problems.
- Becoming more confident learning by speaking and answering questions.

For children who are not currently in school, this gives them access to free learning support. For children already in school, Sabi provides extra practice at their level.

## Purpose of the Pre-Pilot

This pre-pilot will help us understand how to improve Sabi for the future. We want to learn:

- Whether children can learn comfortably through phone calls.
- Whether Sabi explains lessons clearly.
- Whether children enjoy the learning experience.
- What needs to be improved before a larger pilot.

## Duration

The pre-pilot is expected to run for **3 to 6 months**. Participation is voluntary, and parents/guardians may withdraw their child at any time.

## Mode of Delivery

Lessons will be delivered through phone calls.

Parents or children will only need to **flash** the Sabi number. This means they call the number briefly and end the call. Sabi will then call them back for the lesson.

The lesson calls will be **free for the participating child/family**, because Sabi will call back after the flash. Families do not need to buy airtime for the lesson calls.

Each lesson will be short. Parents/guardians will need to give the child the phone for about **5-7 minutes per lesson**.

Some days may include:

- **One 5-7 minute literacy lesson**
- **One 5-7 minute numeracy lesson**

Where possible, these lessons may be separated by a short break.

## Times of Calling

The expected call times are:

- **Out-of-school / market children:** Morning sessions, between **8:00am and 12:00pm**
- **In-school children:** Evening sessions, between **6:00pm and 8:00pm**

Exact timing will be coordinated with parents/guardians.

## Parent/Guardian’s Role

Parents/guardians are asked to:

- Give permission for the child to participate.
- Allow the child to use the phone for about **5-7 minutes per lesson**.
- Help ensure the child is available at the agreed call time.
- Provide a quiet space where possible.
- Encourage the child, without answering for them.
- Share feedback with Education for Equality about the child’s experience.

## Child’s Role

The child will be asked to:

- Speak with Sabi during the phone lesson.
- Listen and try their best.
- Answer Sabi’s questions out loud.
- Ask for help if they do not understand.
- Tell a parent/guardian if they do not want to continue.

## Benefits

By participating, your child may benefit from:

- Learning how to read and write.
- Practising basic mathematics.
- Being part of the first pilot of a state-wide education initiative.
- Receiving free learning support, especially if they are not currently in school.

## Call Recording and Feedback

Some calls may be recorded for learning review, quality improvement, safety, and feedback. These recordings help us understand whether Sabi is hearing children correctly, teaching clearly, and responding appropriately.

At the end of some calls, the child or parent may be invited to leave an optional voice note about the experience.

## Voluntary Participation

Participation is voluntary. Your child can stop participating at any time. Refusing to participate will not affect your child’s schooling, church/community participation, or relationship with Education for Equality.

## Consent Statement

Please tick:

[  ] I understand what Sabi is and how the pre-pilot will work.
[  ] I understand that my child’s participation is voluntary.
[  ] I understand that lessons will happen through free callback phone calls.
[  ] I understand that my child will need the phone for about 5-7 minutes per lesson.
[  ] I understand that some calls may be recorded for quality, safety, and improvement.
[  ] I understand that I can withdraw my child at any time.
[  ] I give permission for my child to participate in the Sabi voice learning pre-pilot.

## Codex · 2026-06-23T22:15:41.678Z · final_answer

Yes, we can build it, and for the pre-pilot I’d do it in a **parent support loop**, not a heavy “parent app.”

**Best Pre-Pilot Setup**
Use three layers:

1. **One-way SMS reminders**
Example:
“Good evening. Remi’s Sabi lesson is open today between 6pm and 8pm. Please flash +234 201 700 1459 and Sabi will call back. Reply on WhatsApp or flash this number if you need help.”

E4E pays to send these.

2. **WhatsApp support for parents who have WhatsApp**
This is the easiest “trusted helper” experience. Parents can message:
“Call did not work”
“Sabi could not hear my child”
“My child was confused”
“Change lesson time”

Their WhatsApp reply does not cost SMS airtime, but it does use mobile data. For parents already using WhatsApp, this is usually fine.

3. **Flash-for-help for everyone**
This is the key for parents without data or WhatsApp. If they have difficulty, they flash the Sabi/support number, and we call them back. That keeps support free/minimal-cost for the parent.

**Will It Cost Them To Text Back?**
- If they reply by normal SMS to a normal number/standard shortcode: **yes, likely normal SMS cost to them**.
- If we get a **toll-free/reverse-billed SMS shortcode**: then **E4E pays**, but that probably needs provider/telco setup and may not be ready for next week.
- If they reply on WhatsApp: no SMS charge, but they need data.
- If they flash and we call back: basically the safest “free to parent” path.

For the pre-pilot, I’d avoid asking parents to “text back” by SMS. Say: **WhatsApp us if you use WhatsApp, or flash us and we will call you back.**

**What I’d Build**
A small parent check-in system:

- Parent/child table: parent name, child name, phone, in-school/out-of-school, preferred window.
- Reminder scheduler: sends SMS/WhatsApp before lesson window.
- Check-in prompts every few days:
  “How is Sabi going for Remi? If there is any problem, WhatsApp us here or flash the Sabi number and we will call back.”
- Missed-call support queue:
  if parent flashes support/Sabi number outside lesson flow, mark as `needs_human_followup`.
- Simple admin dashboard:
  `Parent`, `Child`, `Last lesson`, `Last reminder`, `Issue reported`, `Needs follow-up`.

**My recommendation**
For next week: **SMS reminders + WhatsApp support + flash-for-help callback**.
Later: get a reverse-billed/toll-free SMS shortcode if we need parents on feature phones to text freely.

Sources checked: Africa’s Talking supports toll-free two-way SMS where the owner bears sent/received costs; WhatsApp Business charges businesses per delivered message category, while service messages/customer support windows are treated differently; normal SMS replies can cost the sender unless reverse-billed/toll-free is set up.

## Codex · 2026-06-24T15:53:39.606Z · final_answer

Short answer: **Press One is more expensive than our current Africa’s Talking flash-callback setup for the pre-pilot**, but it may be **competitive for a real 0800/toll-free PBX setup** if their per-minute rates are good.

**Press One fixed cost**
- Annual fee: `₦650,000`
- PBX/SIP setup: `₦250,000`
- First year fixed cost: `₦900,000`
- Effective first-year monthly fixed cost: `₦75,000/month`
- After first year: `₦54,167/month`

**Compared to Africa’s Talking**
Africa’s Talking does not really solve Nigeria toll-free directly for us. Our current AT route is a regular Nigerian DID/SIP number with flash-callback.

For the pre-pilot, AT is much cheaper because we only pay for actual usage:
- Current AT number maintenance is around `₦5,000/month + VAT`
- Callback minutes are the real cost
- For 5-10 children, AT callback usage should be nowhere near `₦900,000`

So for **next week’s pre-pilot**, Press One is overkill.

**Compared to true 0800/toll-free**
Press One is not obviously expensive. It is roughly in the same fixed-cost class as Nigerian 0800/PBX providers.

Our earlier MTN 0800/SIP estimate was:
- Setup: `₦450,000`
- Monthly: `₦37,625`
- First-year fixed: about `₦901,500`
- Plus per-minute charges

So Press One first-year fixed cost, `₦900,000`, is basically the same as that MTN-style estimate.

**Critical missing number**
Ask Press One:

```text
Does the ₦650,000 annual fee include any call minutes?
What is the per-minute rate for inbound toll-free calls?
What is the per-minute rate for outbound callback calls?
Is this an actual 0800 toll-free number, or a regular DID/PBX number?
Does it work from MTN, Airtel, Glo, and 9mobile?
Can it route calls to our SIP trunk/PBX at 136.243.8.51?
How many concurrent calls/channels are included?
```

My decision:
- **For pre-pilot:** stay on AT flash-callback.
- **For serious pilot / cleaner UX:** Press One may be worth considering only if per-minute inbound/outbound is lower than AT and it is truly cross-network toll-free.

## Naomi · 2026-06-25T02:05:17.043Z

show me the plan for that

## Codex · 2026-06-25T02:05:44.345Z · final_answer

**Parent Helper Plan**

Yes. I’d build it in two stages: a simple pre-pilot helper that works immediately, then a more automated parent support system once calls are stable.

**Pre-Pilot Version**
Use this for the first 10 kids:

1. Parent list in Supabase
   Store parent name, phone number, child name, child status, preferred window, consent status, network, and notes.

2. One-way reminders
   Send short SMS/WhatsApp reminders like:

   `Hello from Education for Equality. Please help [Child Name] flash Sabi today at +234 201 700 1459 for their free lesson. Sabi will call back.`

3. Human help channel
   Parents should not text the Sabi lesson number for help. Use:
   - WhatsApp/call Mr. Richard
   - `info@eduforequality.org`
   - Later, a separate support number

4. Parent check-in after 2-3 lessons
   Message:

   `Hello, this is E4E checking in. Has [Child Name] been able to use Sabi? Please reply on WhatsApp or contact Mr. Richard if there was any issue.`

5. Manual support dashboard
   Simple admin view showing:
   - child has/hasn’t called
   - last call time
   - call completed or dropped
   - feedback recording exists
   - parent needs follow-up
   - safety concern flag

**Important Cost Rule**
Do **not** ask parents to reply by normal SMS unless we are okay with them paying. WhatsApp replies only cost data. Normal SMS replies usually cost the parent. Toll-free/reverse-billed SMS would be better later, but probably too slow to set up for the pre-pilot.

**Do Not Use Sabi Number For Help**
If they flash Sabi for support, Sabi may treat it as a lesson call. So for now:

- Sabi number = lessons only
- Richard/WhatsApp/email = help and complaints

**Automated Version**
After the pre-pilot starts working:

1. Daily reminder scheduler
   Sends based on child group:
   - market/out-of-school: morning
   - in-school: afternoon/evening

2. Missed-lesson nudges
   If child has not called in 2 days:

   `Hi, we noticed [Child Name] has not used Sabi recently. Is everything okay? You can reply on WhatsApp or contact Mr. Richard.`

3. Parent issue categories
   Track:
   - call did not connect
   - child could not hear Sabi
   - Sabi could not hear child
   - wrong answer marked incorrectly
   - parent confused about callback
   - safety concern
   - child enjoyed it
   - child does not want to continue

4. Escalation
   Safety concerns and repeated call failures get flagged for Naomi/Richard immediately.

5. Weekly digest
   For Sonia/Richard/you:
   - active children
   - missed lessons
   - parent complaints
   - call quality issues
   - learning progress
   - urgent follow-ups

My recommendation: build **Parent Helper v0** as WhatsApp-first + one-way SMS + admin tracking, then add automation once the first few families are actually calling.

## Codex · 2026-06-25T18:11:58.393Z · commentary

I found it: Sabi already has API-key support wired in. The key is read from `sabi-server/secrets/SABI_API_KEY` through Docker secrets, and the admin endpoints accept it as either `X-API-Key` or `?api_key=...`.

## Codex · 2026-06-25T18:12:01.644Z · final_answer

For Sabi, make the API key by creating this secret file on the server:

```bash
ssh root@136.243.8.51
cd /opt/sabi/sabi-server
mkdir -p secrets
openssl rand -hex 32 > secrets/SABI_API_KEY
chmod 600 secrets/SABI_API_KEY
docker compose up -d --force-recreate sabi
```

Then read it only when you need to open the backend:

```bash
cat /opt/sabi/sabi-server/secrets/SABI_API_KEY
```

Use it like:

```text
/admin/review?api_key=[REDACTED:sensitive-label]
```

or as a header:

```bash
curl -H "X-API-Key: [REDACTED:header-credential]" http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/learners
```

Tiny important thing: don’t paste this key into docs, GitHub, or emails. If it leaks, just rerun the `openssl rand...` command and restart Sabi to rotate it.

## Codex · 2026-06-26T17:48:59.143Z · commentary

The GitHub thing was **GitHub Actions**: a workflow file like `.github/workflows/deploy-sabi.yml`.

Important distinction: I would set it up to **auto-deploy after you intentionally push to GitHub**, not auto-push every local edit. Auto-pushing every edit is how regressions sneak into production. The clean version is:

1. You or Codex commits/pushes.
2. GitHub Actions runs tests.
3. If tests pass, it SSHes into the Sabi server and deploys.
4. If tests fail, it stops before touching the live phone system.

On streaming: right now Sabi is “streaming audio” at the phone layer, but **not streaming STT**. Asterisk sends live audio to our server, Sabi can interrupt, but we still collect one user utterance, save it as a WAV, then send that clip to Groq/Whisper. That means Sabi only knows what you said after the turn ends.

**Streaming STT** means we send tiny audio chunks while you’re still talking and get partial transcripts back live. Benefits:
- faster response after you stop talking
- better endpointing, because the STT service can detect speech/silence
- possible live confidence/partial text
- can feel more like ChatGPT voice

But streaming is a bigger architecture risk. For Intron specifically, the safer first merge is **file-upload STT for each short turn** behind `SABI_LITERACY_STT_PROVIDER=intron`. That lets us compare Intron vs Groq/Whisper on real Sabi clips without destabilizing calls. If it clearly hears Nigerian/literacy speech better, then we can move to streaming STT for latency. Accuracy and latency are separate: Intron may hear your voice more clearly because of accent/domain training; streaming mainly makes it respond faster.

## Codex · 2026-06-26T17:52:05.920Z · commentary

GitHub Actions is GitHub’s built-in automation runner. Think: “when code is pushed, run these commands.” It can run tests, build, deploy to the server, make releases, or back things up. It is not the same thing as GitHub storage itself.

For freeing up space on your computer, the thing you were probably talking about is:

- **push everything to GitHub remotes**: put each project/repo safely on GitHub
- optionally use **Git LFS**: for large model/audio/video/data files that normal Git should not store
- then clean local copies only after confirming GitHub has them
- optionally archive old project folders into cloud storage/OneDrive if they are not code repos

GitHub Actions would help *after* that by automating “test and deploy when pushed,” but it does not by itself free space. The “GitHub thing” for storage is just **GitHub repositories**, plus **Git LFS** if there are big binary files.

For Sabi specifically:
- `sabi-server` is its own git repo.
- `curriculum-app` is its own git repo.
- The safest setup is: push both cleanly to GitHub, add `.gitignore`/LFS for big audio/cache/model artifacts, then add GitHub Actions for Sabi deploys.

I would not delete anything local until we run a repo-by-repo audit showing:
1. what is tracked,
2. what is untracked,
3. what is too large for normal Git,
4. what has actually been pushed to GitHub.

Done. Sabi is deployed again and healthy.

I cleaned the admin UI in [admin_review.py](/Users/naomiivie/Education%20for%20Equality/sabi-server/admin_review.py): recent conversations now have clear `Length` / `Child turns` labels, cleaner Open/Saved states, less raw-log feeling, and centered curriculum map labels so the map reads better.

That should help short letter/sound answers get picked up.

I also fixed the optional Intron STT wiring in [stt.py](/Users/naomiivie/Education%20for%20Equality/sabi-server/stt.py): Intron stays behind `SABI_LITERACY_STT_PROVIDER=intron`, uses the correct `Authorization: Bearer ...` auth from their docs, and falls back to Groq/Whisper if it fails. It is **not enabled live yet**. Live logs still show Groq Whisper.

On Intron/streaming: Intron looks worth A/B testing for Nigerian/African accented speech, but I would not blindly replace Whisper. Their docs expose file upload sync and WebSocket streaming; streaming can make Sabi respond faster because partial transcripts arrive while the child is still talking, but it is a bigger architecture change than the safe per-turn file upload path. Sources: [Intron file upload sync](https://docs.voice.intron.io/docs/stt/file-upload-sync), [Intron streaming](https://docs.voice.intron.io/docs/stt/streaming), [supported languages](https://docs.voice.intron.io/docs/stt/supported-languages).

Verified on production:
`/health` is OK, admin review regression passes, phone runtime regression passes, STT provider regression passes, and STT normalizer regression is `12/12`.

## Codex · 2026-06-26T19:05:36.564Z · commentary

## Codex · 2026-06-26T19:05:56.254Z · final_answer

Current code splits by **call**, not inside one long mixed lesson.

Right now, Sabi is set up to alternate:
- One call = literacy lesson
- Next call = numeracy lesson
- Next call = literacy again

So for the pre-pilot, I’d do **two short calls per day**, not one 12-minute mixed call.

Recommended order:
1. **Literacy first, 5-7 minutes**
   Because sound/rhyme/word listening needs the child’s freshest attention and quietest environment.
2. **Short break, even 2-5 minutes**
3. **Numeracy second, 5-7 minutes**
   Numeracy can tolerate a bit more fatigue because market/money problems are more concrete.

Sabi should explicitly say it. Right now she says things like “sound game,” but not clearly enough. I’d change the opening to:

For literacy:
“Today we’re starting your reading and sounds lesson. We’ll play a short word and sound game.”

For numeracy:
“Now we’re starting your maths lesson. We’ll practise numbers and money problems.”

At the end of the first call:
“Great work on literacy. Take a short break. When you call again, we’ll do maths.”

This is cleaner than doing both subjects inside one call, and it makes the admin data easier too: each call has one learning goal.

It now lands on an **Overview / Launch Control** page instead of dumping people straight into raw rows. It shows review queue, learners needing attention, pre-pilot readiness, and the backend model we are copying from serious AI/product/edtech systems. Asterisk/phone routing was untouched.

**Substantial Summary**
The big lesson from OpenAI/Anthropic/Groq is: new AI product paths should not be launched because they “feel better.” They move through explicit gates.

OpenAI-style: system cards, internal evals, external red-teamers/domain experts, risk categories, mitigations, and post-launch monitoring.

Anthropic-style: written deployment thresholds, Responsible Scaling Policy logic, no-go gates, safeguards before release, and external vulnerability testing.

Groq-style: production readiness around latency, timeouts, retries, rate limits, cost, error rate, p95/p99 latency, and STT debugging metadata.

For Sabi, that becomes:

1. Baseline current working system.
2. Offline replay saved call clips.
3. Isolated route, like the Intron `9020` lane.
4. Adult canary calls.
5. Tiny child canary, starting with 2 children.
6. 10-child pre-pilot.
7. Promote only if evidence beats baseline.
8. Roll back fast if STT, latency, wrong grading, call drops, or safety gets worse.

For the backend, the best analogs were not generic dashboards. They were learning-ops consoles:

- Khan Academy: student rows, assignments/sessions, responses, completion, export.
- Lexia Core5: “who needs help,” “who needs more time,” risk signals, recommended next action.
- IXL: diagnostics, skills practiced, cohort/admin analytics.
- Seesaw: student evidence, family/admin visibility, progress monitoring.

So Sabi’s admin console has to be better than normal edtech because it must show both **learning evidence** and **voice-AI evidence**: child audio, what Sabi heard, normalized transcript, Sabi reply, TTS text, call quality, curriculum position, and next action.

Verification passed:
- `https://api.eduforequality.org/health` is OK.
- Container `admin_review_regression.py` passed.
- Live admin HTML contains the new Overview, Review Queue, and backend model sections.

Key sources: [OpenAI external testing](https://openai.com/index/strengthening-safety-with-external-testing/), [OpenAI GPT-4o system card](https://openai.com/index/gpt-4o-system-card/), [Anthropic RSP](https://www.anthropic.com/news/announcing-our-updated-responsible-scaling-policy), [Groq production checklist](https://console.groq.com/docs/production-readiness/production-ready-checklist), [Khan teacher reports](https://support.khanacademy.org/hc/en-us/articles/38554738905997-What-teacher-reports-are-available-on-Khan-Academy-Reimagined), [Lexia Core5 reports](https://community.lexialearning.com/student-progress-reports-97/mylexia-reports-core5-class-overview-1554), [IXL Analytics](https://www.ixl.com/help-center/article/1259753/how_can_i_find_an_ixl_analytics_report_that_best_suits_my_needs), [Seesaw platform](https://seesaw.com/products/all-in-one-platform/).
